ARREARS::transferee-liability.code: Electricity Act / Supply Codes (general principle; cf. Clause 4.3(g)&(h))
ARREARS::transferee-liability.topic: Arrears are not a charge; transferee liable only where statutory rules/terms so provide

cases.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cases.topic: Arrears are not a charge; transferee liable only where statutory rules/terms so provide
cases.holding: (i) Electricity arrears do not constitute a charge over the property, so in general law a transferee cannot be made liable for the previous owner/occupier's dues. (ii) But where statutory rules, or statutory terms and conditions of supply, authorise the supplier to demand the previous owner's arrears from a purchaser seeking re-/fresh connection, the supplier may recover them. Here the Board pleaded no such enabling provision (introduced in Haryana only in 2001), so the demand against the auction-purchaser failed.
cases.flag: Multi-state (Haryana) and general-law principle; the doctrinal foundation of the arrears/transferee cluster (cf. SCJ-005 K.C. Ninan, SCJ-012). The Court expressly notes that provisions like Clause 4.3(g) & (h) of an Electricity Supply Code are necessary to enable such recovery.

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Supply Code can create a statutory charge for a previous owner's arrears recoverable from a new owner (apex authority)
cases.holding: Yes. A condition of supply requiring the new owner to clear the previous owner's arrears has a statutory character (s.49, 1948 Act); the State Commission's regulatory power under s.50, and the rule-making power under s.181 read with s.50, are wide enough to stipulate recovery of a previous owner's arrears from a new/subsequent owner and to create a statutory charge on the premises even where the plenary statute does not provide for one. Such Supply Code recoupment has a reasonable nexus with the objects of the 2003 Act. The power to recover by suit is independent of the disconnection power under s.56; and 'as is where is' puts an auction-purchaser on notice of electricity dues. Outstanding interest from the date of the supply application was waived under Article 142.
cases.flag: Apex authority confirming the arrears/transferee line (cf. SCJ-031 Haryana SEB; applied in SCJ-005 Amir Ahmad). Substantially qualifies Isha Marbles (1995).

cases.title: M/S Dharti Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. The Managing Director, Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.topic: IBC Section 238 overrides the Electricity Act/Supply Code first-charge and arrears-recovery provisions where the premises were acquired via IBC liquidation and the licensee has submitted its claim to the Liquidator
cases.holding: No. Section 238 of the IBC — a subsequent, non-obstante special enactment — overrides Sections 173-174 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and Clause 4.3(f)(iv) of the Supply Code (first charge on assets), following Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat (P) Ltd. and Southern Power Distribution Co. of Telangana v. Gopal Agarwal. Once the licensee has participated in the liquidation and lodged its claim, it cannot also insist on payment of the arrears as a precondition for a fresh connection to the auction-purchaser; its dues are recoverable only through the IBC Section 53 waterfall mechanism via the Liquidator, not by withholding supply. K.C. Ninan's holding that a Supply Code condition can make arrears run with the premises is confined to its own facts (no IBC liquidation in issue) and does not apply once the IBC framework and the licensee's own participation in it are engaged. The impugned demand/refusal order was set aside and the licensee directed to install the connection, retaining liberty to recover its dues only from the Liquidator.

cases.title: Palika Towns LLP v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Survey and application, by analogy, of the electricity-dues transferee-liability doctrine (dues do not constitute a charge absent specific stipulation) to hold an IBC-auction purchaser of an industrial leasehold liable for the corporate debtor's pre-existing lease-rent arrears, given an express 'first charge' clause in the lease deed and the purchaser's acceptance of the Transfer Memorandum/Sale Certificate
cases.holding: Yes. Surveying the electricity-dues transferee-liability line (Haryana SEB v. Hanuman Rice Mills; Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam v. DVS Steels & Alloys; Telangana State Southern Power Distribution Co.), the Court summarized the settled position: such dues do not themselves constitute a charge over the property, so a transferee is not automatically liable absent a specific statutory/regulatory stipulation authorising recovery from a purchaser, or an auction notice expressly flagging the dues as the purchaser's liability. Applying this by analogy, the Court found the lease deed here contained an express first-charge clause (Clause 3(b), Chapter IV) covering unpaid lease rent/interest/other dues, which displaced the general Transfer of Property Act s.55(1)(g) rule (applicable only 'in absence of a contract to the contrary'); the purchaser had also signed the Transfer Memorandum and accepted the Sale Certificate incorporating the lease covenants, and could not now approbate and reprobate by accepting the beneficial parts of those instruments while disclaiming the burden. GNIDA's failure to register its claim in the IBC liquidation proceedings did not extinguish its right to demand the arrears as a condition of transfer/recognition of the purchaser as lessee. Refund of the amount paid under protest was accordingly refused.

CPC::res-judicata.topic: Second suit on a different subject-matter/relief not barred

cases.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cases.topic: Second suit on a different subject-matter/relief not barred
cases.holding: The second suit (challenging the 1998 disconnection threat and disconnection for the previous owner's arrears) was not barred by res judicata by the dismissal of the earlier suit (for a permanent injunction against the 1995 demand), the matters directly in issue and the reliefs being different.

EA1999(UP)::26.clause: s.26 (Commission's power to enforce licence conditions/tariff compliance) vis-a-vis s.48 (bar of civil suits)
EA1999(UP)::26.topic: An application alleging that a licensee is charging a surcharge inconsistent with an approved tariff order (violating licence terms/tariff compliance) is properly filed under s.26 of the 1999 Act before the Commission, not a barred civil suit

cases.title: Northern Coalfield Ltd. v. Chairman and Managing Director, U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: An application alleging that a licensee is charging a surcharge inconsistent with an approved tariff order (violating licence terms/tariff compliance) is properly filed under s.26 of the 1999 Act before the Commission, not a barred civil suit
cases.holding: Since a civil suit is barred under s.48 of the 1999 Act, and the consumer's grievance was in substance that the licensee was contravening the terms and conditions of its licence/tariff order by levying an unauthorised surcharge, the application was properly maintainable under s.26 (not Regulation 138's 90-day review-application bar, which did not apply).

EA2003::126.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (read with the DERC Supply Code Regulations)
EA2003::126.topic: Legal fiction of 'deemed' consumption under the Supply Code / s.126 must be given full effect

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.topic: Legal fiction of 'deemed' consumption under the Supply Code / s.126 must be given full effect
cases.holding: Yes. Where the statute and the DERC Supply Code Regulations create a legal fiction that assessed energy is 'deemed' consumed (e.g. under the LDHF formula), the fiction must be taken to its logical end: the assessed units must be treated as 'sales'. The DERC's method of back-calculating units from the reduced settlement amount is contrary to law; assessed energy is to be considered as supply, with the impact and carrying costs allowed.

cases.title: Islam v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Agricultural ancillary use (kolhu) within sanctioned load is not unauthorised use
cases.holding: No. Ancillary use of a sanctioned agricultural connection for a kolhu/kutti machine to crush one's own produce, within the sanctioned load, is authorised agricultural use (per the licensee's own policy order of 11.11.2005), not unauthorised use — unless the load exceeds the sanctioned load or a second meter is installed. The burden to prove commercial use/theft is on the department; absent any allegation of crushing for others/hire, excess load, or a second meter, the assessment is illegal and quashed.

cases.title: Kapil Gupta v. U.P. Power Corpn. Ltd. & Anr.
cases.topic: A Section 126 assessment can be made even in a theft case
cases.holding: Section 126 (Chapter XII, investigation/enforcement) empowers a provisional assessment of charges for unauthorised use, while Section 135 (Chapter XIV, offences) makes unauthorised use a criminal offence; the two operate in different chapters, and a person committing theft/unauthorised use still bears the civil liability to pay for the consumption. A provisional assessment can therefore be made in a theft case.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.topic: Sections 126 and 135 are distinct provisions in different fields; s.126 is civil and intention-neutral
cases.holding: No commonality. Sections 126 and 135 operate in different and distinct fields. Section 135 falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is a relevant factor for theft; Section 126 does not speak of any criminal intendment and is primarily a civil remedy, applying even in the absence of intention.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.topic: 'Unauthorised use' is a wider, purposively-construed expression covering excess load
cases.holding: 'Unauthorised use of electricity' is an expression of wider connotation, to be construed purposively rather than restrictively by the clauses of the Explanation, keeping in mind the object and purpose of the Act. Consumption in excess of the maximum contracted/sanctioned load falls under Explanation (b)(iv) to Section 126 (besides violating the Regulations and the agreement of supply).

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Theft (s.135) is a subset of unauthorised use (s.126); a s.126 assessment is available even in theft cases
cases.holding: Yes. All instances of unauthorised use may not amount to theft, but theft under Section 135 falls within the definition of 'unauthorised use of electricity'; use through a tampered meter is therefore unauthorised use assessable under Section 126(6)(b)(iii). The authorities are empowered to make a provisional and final assessment under Section 126(1) even in cases where electricity is unauthorisedly used by way of theft.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.topic: Law applicable to the deposit condition and assessment rate is the law in force on the date of the FINAL assessment, not the date of provisional assessment or the underlying cause of action
cases.holding: The amended Act governs. A provisional assessment is not a final assessment and carries no independent right of appeal; the cause of action for the statutory appeal arises only from the final assessment. The law prevailing on the date of the final assessment (here, 2011) applies both to the deposit condition for the appeal and to the assessment rate under Section 126(6) (amended to 'twice' the tariff, from 'one-and-half times'), regardless of when the theft/cause of action arose (2004) or the provisional assessment was made.

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: CGRF and Ombudsman have no jurisdiction over Section 126 unauthorised-use assessments or Section 127 appellate orders — a parallel forum by subordinate legislation is impermissible
cases.holding: No. The Assessing Officer under Section 126 is a statutory authority and his order is appealable only under Section 127; where the statute itself creates its own adjudicatory and appellate forum, a parallel forum created by subordinate legislation (CGRF/Ombudsman under the 2007 Regulations) is not permissible and has no jurisdiction at all over such assessments. An earlier writ order that had allowed the consumer to approach CGRF, without the jurisdictional point being raised or contested, does not confer jurisdiction — a judgment lays down a ratio decidendi only on an issue raised, argued and decided, and jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or a court's assumption. The entire CGRF and Ombudsman proceedings (including the order refunding Rs. 14.44 lakh with 16% compound interest) were quashed as a nullity, with liberty to the consumer to pursue objections before the Assessing Officer under Section 126 or an appeal under Section 127, condoning any resulting delay if availed within one month.

cases.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Physical/MRI indicators suffice to ground a theft inference; Ashok Kumar's notice requirement satisfied by the checking report's own disclosed facts
cases.holding: No. A naked conductor found at the LT mains bracket, a broken seal, and an MRI report showing an unexplained wide variance in the power-factor ratio and a reversed phase sequence (which cannot occur without manual manipulation) together well-support the Assessing Officer's inference of direct extraction/theft; this is not a case of no evidence. Ashok Kumar requires only that the consumer be informed of the manner in which he is alleged to have committed theft so he can respond — satisfied here since the checking report itself discloses, under 'observations', the facts from which theft is inferred, even though the consumer was not caught red-handed. No error in the actual quantum of assessment was pointed out.

cases.title: M/S Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
cases.topic: Where the Code's assessment-rate provision conflicts with the statute, the statute prevails
cases.holding: At the relevant date, Section 126(6) fixed the assessment rate at one-and-a-half times the applicable tariff; any discrepancy in the Code (which the assessing/appellate authorities read as permitting a rate of thrice/twice respectively) must yield to the statute, which prevails over the Code in case of conflict. Both the assessing officer's (thrice) and the appellate authority's (twice) orders were accordingly unsustainable on rate alone, independent of the Clause 5.6 defect.

cases.title: Navi Hasan v. U.P. Power Corporation & Another
cases.topic: A pre-printed, non-speaking demand order passed in defiance of prior court directions to confront the consumer with adverse material and pass a reasoned order after hearing violates natural justice and is quashed with costs; an officer's unexplained recall/withdrawal of such an order mid-litigation, without disclosing statutory basis, is prima facie misconduct
cases.holding: No — the impugned order dated 21.3.2022 was found to be a pre-printed order (only name, checking-report number, notice number, and the demanded amount of Rs. 5,19,525/- filled in by hand), issued in conscious disregard of this Court's earlier order dated 22.10.2021 (Writ-C No. 26241 of 2021) requiring disclosure of adverse material, an opportunity for objections, a hearing, and a reasoned order. This violated the audi alteram partem principle and the order was quashed, with a direction to confront the petitioner with adverse material afresh, permit objections, and pass a reasoned assessment order after a hearing, all within a defined timeline. Costs of Rs. 1,00,000/- were imposed on the respondent officer given the deliberate defiance of the court's earlier directions, compounded by an unexplained mid-litigation withdrawal/recall of the impugned order without disclosing the statutory power under the Electricity Act or Supply Code to do so.

cases.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Section 126 assessment must be made even in theft (s.135) cases with a pending Special Court trial; the Special Court's civil-liability jurisdiction under s.154(5)/(6) operates alongside, not instead of, the assessing officer's s.126 process — 'unauthorised use of electricity' is the genus of which theft is a dishonest species
cases.holding: (1)-(2) Yes, s.126 assessment must be made even in theft cases pending Special Court trial. 'Unauthorised use of electricity' under Explanation (b) to s.126 is a wide genus comprehensively covering theft under s.135 as a dishonest species of the same conduct; the sixth proviso to s.135(1), which conditions restoration of supply on payment of the 'assessed amount', itself presupposes a s.126 assessment exists to be paid. Clause 8.1 of the Supply Code, 2005 (framed by the Regulatory Commission under s.50) confirms this understanding by prescribing a provisional-assessment-and-hearing procedure specifically for theft cases under s.135. The now-omitted Clause 8.0(6) (allowing interim-payment restoration pending Special Court decision) was merely an option for restoration, not an indication that s.126 assessment is inapplicable to theft. The Special Court's role under s.154(5)/(6) is to finally determine civil liability (which may differ from — and trigger refund/adjustment against — the s.126-assessed amount already deposited), not to displace the assessing officer's s.126 jurisdiction. Following Paliwal Alloys, Radha Krishna Cold Storage, Ashok Kumar, Mohit Paper Mills, and distinguishing the Andhra Pradesh High Court's Tirumala Modern Rice Mill and clarifying that the Supreme Court's Southco v. Seetaram Rice Mill (holding ss.126/135 operate in 'different fields') did not hold that s.126 assessment is barred in theft cases: (i) assessment under s.126 is to be made even where a s.135 offence is pending trial before the Special Court; (ii) the Special Court finally determines civil liability, with s.154(6) governing any refund if that determination is less than the amount already deposited pursuant to s.126 assessment.

EA2003::126(3).topic: Personal hearing is part of 'reasonable opportunity' before a final theft assessment

cases.title: Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Personal hearing is part of 'reasonable opportunity' before a final theft assessment
cases.holding: It requires a personal hearing. Merely taking note of written objections is not compliance; because supply (an essential service) has been disconnected and the theft charge carries penal consequences, a personal hearing is essential before a final assessment. The ex parte final assessment is quashed and remitted for a fresh reasoned order after personal hearing, conditioned on the consumer depositing 50% of the claim (25% cash + 25% security).

EA2003::126(5).topic: Assessment period — entire period of unauthorised use, or 12 months if unascertainable

cases.title: Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Assessment period — entire period of unauthorised use, or 12 months if unascertainable
cases.holding: Section 126(5) has two parts: assessment for the entire period during which unauthorised use took place, or, if that period cannot be ascertained, a period limited to twelve months preceding inspection. Whether the period (here 407 days) was properly ascertained is a factual question for the assessing/appellate authority.

EA2003::127.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (transition from U.P. Supply (Consumers) Regulations 1984 / U.P. Supply Code 2002)
EA2003::127.topic: Scope of the Section 127 appeal — confined to Section 126 orders; transitional assessments

cases.title: Aruna Bhargava v. PuVVNL & Another
cases.topic: Scope of the Section 127 appeal — confined to Section 126 orders; transitional assessments
cases.holding: No. Section 127(1) confines the appeal to a final order 'made under Section 126' of the 2003 Act; a pre-2003 assessment is not such an order, so neither Section 127 nor its pre-deposit condition applies. Section 185(2) & (5) (with Section 6 of the General Clauses Act) preserve the pre-2003 assessment and its appellate forum. The Commissioner's rejection under s.127(2) was without jurisdiction; the appeal is remitted to the forum under Regulations 1984 / Code 2002.
cases.flag: Multi-regime transitional case: it construes the pre-2005 U.P. regime (Regulations 1984 and U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2002), not the 2005 Code.

cases.title: Kapil Gupta v. U.P. Power Corpn. Ltd. & Anr.
cases.topic: Writ relegated to the statutory appeal where only factual disputes arise
cases.holding: Relegated to the appeal. Where the challenge to a Section 126 assessment raises only disputed questions of fact and no question of jurisdiction, vires, or breach of natural justice/fundamental rights, the writ court will not bypass the Section 127 appeal; the earlier decision on merits in this consumer's case turned on a four-year pendency, not any absolute rule, and Ashok Kumar (vires/jurisdiction) is distinguishable.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.topic: Sections 126-127 form a complete code; only a final Section 126(3) order is appealable; the High Court should not ordinarily interfere with a final assessment
cases.holding: Sections 126 and 127 together constitute a complete code. Only a final order of assessment under Section 126(3) is appealable under Section 127; a notice-cum-provisional assessment under Section 126(2) is not appealable. The High Court should normally decline to interfere under Article 226 with a final assessment — it may examine a jurisdictional challenge but must not travel into the assessing officer's exclusive domain of assessment and fact-finding.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.topic: Challenge to a final theft assessment relegated to the statutory appeal; pre-deposit not relaxed
cases.holding: Whether inspection or provisional assessment was properly made, and whether reasonable opportunity was given, are matters merged into the earlier writ proceeding that directed consideration of the representation (itself equivalent to the provisional stage) and cannot be reopened by a fresh writ against the final assessment; the final assessment must be challenged before the appellate authority under Section 127, and in a theft matter — given the public interest in the essential service of electricity — the Court will not relax the statutory deposit condition to enable the petitioner to avoid it.

cases.title: M/S Om Ice Factory Thru' Its Partner Satyapal Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr.
cases.topic: Where an assessment challenge is purely factual/procedural (objections already considered) and raises no jurisdictional or vires issue, the writ is relegated to the s.127 appeal
cases.holding: The petitioner must be relegated to the Section 127 appeal. None of the three recognised exceptions to the alternative-remedy rule (want of jurisdiction, breach of natural justice, violation of fundamental rights) was made out: the assessing authority had already considered the petitioner's objections as directed in an earlier writ (disposed of 6.8.2013) and taken a decision not shown to be dehors the law or established procedure; mere allegation of a factual/procedural flaw in that decision does not permit bypassing the statutory remedy. Ashok Kumar is distinguishable since it involved a pure legal/jurisdictional challenge (validity of the notification appointing the assessing officer) that neither the assessing officer nor the appellate authority could decide — here, by contrast, only the correctness of the provisional assessment on facts was at issue. The governing precedent is Southco v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill: the High Court may examine a jurisdictional challenge to a provisional assessment but must remand rather than decide the assessment itself, and should normally decline to interfere with a final assessment under Article 226.

cases.title: M/S Trikoot Iron & Steels Castings Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: A theft-based assessment is made under Section 126 (via Clause 8.1-8.3 of the Code), not Section 135, and is always appealable under Section 127
cases.holding: An appeal always lies. Section 135 creates the criminal offence of theft but no independent assessment mechanism; its third proviso to sub-section (1A) (requiring restoration of supply on deposit of the 'assessed amount') itself presupposes that the assessment is made under Section 126. The Supply Code merely prescribes distinct procedures — para 8.1-8.3 for theft-based assessments, para 6.8 for other unauthorised use — but both are Section 126 assessments; the appeal lies under Section 127 in either case. Since Section 127 provides no separate parameters for deciding the appeal, the Appellate Authority's power is co-extensive with the Assessing Officer's, empowering it to examine on the merits whether the assessment (theft or otherwise) was correctly made. The Appellate Authority's rejection of the appeal on the ground that a theft-based assessment falls under Section 135 (and is hence non-appealable) was a jurisdictional error; the matter was remanded for decision on merits.

EA2003::135.topic: Proof standard: civil for s.126 assessment, beyond reasonable doubt + mens rea for s.135 theft

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Proof standard: civil for s.126 assessment, beyond reasonable doubt + mens rea for s.135 theft
cases.holding: To prove theft in a criminal proceeding the case must be proved beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea established; such strict proof is not necessary for assessing liability under Section 126(1), which requires only civil proof.

cases.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Mens rea not required for a Section 126 civil assessment
cases.holding: The question of mens rea does not arise for a Section 126 assessment on an allegation of theft, since that assessment does not require criminal intention; mens rea is required only for prosecution under Section 135. (Agreeing with Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL, distinguishing Ram Chandra Prasad Sharma v. State of Bihar, which concerned criminal prosecution under the 1910 Act.)

cases.title: Mobin Ahamad v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: FIR disclosing a cognizable s.135 offence will not be quashed, but arrest must follow Cr.P.C. s.41(1)(b)/41-A safeguards, and a compoundable offence's remedy lies via the Supply Code/s.152, not quashing
cases.holding: No — the FIR discloses a cognizable offence and will not be quashed merely because the alleged offence attracts less than 7 years' imprisonment or is compoundable. However, since the sentence would not exceed 7 years, any arrest must comply with the safeguards under Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A of the Cr.P.C.; if the offence is compoundable, the accused may seek his remedy under the provisions of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and Section 152 of the Electricity Act, 2003.

cases.title: Mohamad Aslam v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: Companion ruling to SCJ-081 (Mobin Ahamad) — identical holding on a parallel FIR from the same investigation
cases.holding: As in SCJ-081: the FIR discloses a cognizable offence and is not quashed; any arrest must comply with Cr.P.C. s.41(1)(b)/41-A since the offence would not entail more than 7 years' imprisonment; a compoundable offence's remedy lies under the Supply Code, 2005 and s.152 of the Act.
cases.flag: Near-verbatim companion order to SCJ-081; recorded compactly to avoid duplicating the identical reasoning.

cases.title: Pawan Kumar Laur v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: A licensee's authorised officer is competent under s.135(2) to lodge an FIR for theft of electricity; the FIR is not quashed absent ex-facie absence of a cognizable offence or proven malafide
cases.holding: Yes, the officer is competent under s.135(2), which empowers an authorised officer of the licensee to enter, inspect, search and seize in relation to unauthorised use of electricity, supporting the officer's authority to also lodge an FIR under s.135(1). No malafide was made out merely from the FIR's timing relative to the related writ petition (which had only resulted in notice being issued, not a stay of recovery); the FIR disclosed a prima facie cognizable offence (theft found on inspection, and substantial dues outstanding), and following the settled Bhajan Lal/Satya Pal/Ajit Singh line, courts do not interfere with investigation or quash an FIR absent ex-facie absence of a cognizable offence or a statutory bar on investigation.

EA2003::145.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with Supply Code 2005 & CGRF Regulations 2007)
EA2003::145.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's tort claim (Lok Adalat)

cases.title: Divisional Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-I v. Raman Singh & Another
cases.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's tort claim (Lok Adalat)
cases.holding: For a consumer's dispute, the Act and the Supply Code are comprehensive and civil-court jurisdiction is barred by Section 145. A non-consumer's claim for tort damages against the licensee is not a Code/CGRF matter; 'supply of power' is a 'public utility service' under Section 22-A of the LSA Act, 1987, so the Permanent Lok Adalat has jurisdiction, and the CGRF/Ombudsman Regulations, 2007 (covering only consumer grievances) do not apply. The compensation award is upheld.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's electrocution-damages claim (Lok Adalat)
cases.holding: Yes. 'Public utility service' (LSA Act s.22-A) means supply of power to the public and needs no consumer relationship; the Permanent Lok Adalat has adjudicatory power under s.22-C(8) where conciliation fails. A consumer's electricity dispute is cognizable only by the statutory authorities under the Act/Code, civil-court jurisdiction being barred by Section 145; but a non-consumer's tort claim for electrocution is a civil dispute the Lok Adalat may decide, and a weaker-section claimant cannot be relegated to a civil suit.

EA2003::152.topic: Compounding of electricity theft — whether a pending prosecution is required

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Compounding of electricity theft — whether a pending prosecution is required
cases.holding: Section 152(2) and (3) operate at different stages: under s.152(2), where no criminal proceeding has yet been instituted, payment of the compounding sum sets the person at liberty and bars institution of proceedings; s.152(3) (acceptance deemed an acquittal) applies only where a prosecution is already pending. Compounding therefore does not require a pending prosecution.
cases.flag: The judgment refers throughout to 'Section 152(2) of the Electricity Supply Code 2005'; Section 152 is in the Electricity Act, 2003. Recorded, not merged.

cases.title: Om Prakash s/o Gauri Shankar v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Compounding of a theft offence under s.152(3) does not exonerate the consumer from separate civil liability for electricity consumption dues; a quantum dispute over such recovery must go to the Supply Code authority, not the writ court
cases.holding: No — the compounding fee is a penalty for the criminal offence of theft and does not exonerate the consumer from the separate civil liability to pay for electricity actually consumed; a recovery notice for such dues is not barred by compounding. Any grievance as to the quantum of such dues must be raised before the authority under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, not by way of writ petition.

EA2003::154.topic: The Section 126 assessment and the Special Court's Section 154(5) civil-liability determination are not parallel/mutually exclusive — both may proceed

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: The Section 126 assessment and the Special Court's Section 154(5) civil-liability determination are not parallel/mutually exclusive — both may proceed
cases.holding: The Section 126(1) assessment power and the power to determine civil liability under Section 154(5) are not parallel to each other; the High Court erred in holding the two proceedings cannot operate parallelly. Where there is no theft (only unauthorised use), the loss is assessed under Section 126(1) alone; where the unauthorised use amounts to theft, a Section 126(1) assessment AND a Section 135 complaint may both proceed, with the Special Court determining civil liability under Section 154(5) and any excess deposit refunded. Merely because the Special Court is empowered to determine civil liability under Section 154(5) does not mean the authorities lack power to make a Section 126 assessment.

EA2003::173.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.173, 174) vis-a-vis Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (s.238, s.53 waterfall mechanism)
EA2003::173.clause: ss.173/174 (non-obstante overriding clauses) vis-a-vis IBC s.238 (later, overriding non-obstante clause) and s.53 (liquidation waterfall)
EA2003::173.topic: IBC s.238 overrides the Electricity Act's ss.173/174 recovery mechanism once liquidation has commenced; a distribution licensee cannot independently attach/auction a corporate debtor's property for electricity dues outside the IBC process, and its dues do not automatically rank as 'government dues' merely due to state shareholding, though they may be a 'secured interest' on the facts

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Private Limited & Ors.
cases.topic: IBC s.238 overrides the Electricity Act's ss.173/174 recovery mechanism once liquidation has commenced; a distribution licensee cannot independently attach/auction a corporate debtor's property for electricity dues outside the IBC process, and its dues do not automatically rank as 'government dues' merely due to state shareholding, though they may be a 'secured interest' on the facts
cases.holding: (a) No — s.238 of the IBC, being the later special enactment expressly covering corporate insolvency/liquidation, overrides ss.173/174 of the Electricity Act, 2003 despite the latter's non-obstante clauses; once liquidation commences, the licensee cannot independently attach or auction the corporate debtor's property outside the IBC's collective process, and the District Collector's attachment/auction notice for electricity dues was accordingly set aside, with the property released to the liquidator per the NCLT/NCLAT's order. (b) No — dues payable to a distribution licensee, even one with government shareholding, do not fall within s.53(1)(f)'s 'government dues' description, since such licensees are distinct juristic entities carrying on a liberalised activity open to private participation, and are not 'the State Government' merely by virtue of shareholding or historical function. (c) Not automatically — but on the facts here, given the supply agreement's clause making outstanding dues 'a charge on the assets of the company' and the concurrent, unchallenged NCLT/NCLAT findings that PVVNL was a secured creditor, PVVNL's claim proceeds within the s.53 waterfall as a secured creditor's claim (not outside/above the IBC process), to be verified and processed by the liquidator within 10 weeks. State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers, which treated a statutory first-charge as automatically conferring secured-creditor priority, was confined to its facts — it neither considered the s.53 waterfall nor arose in a liquidation (as opposed to resolution-plan) context, and cannot be extended to elevate electricity/quasi-government dues above Parliament's deliberately structured priority.

EA2003::174.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with s.50; Supply Code Para 7.10 / 7.7.1-7.7.5)
EA2003::174.topic: Overriding effect of the Act does not oust Lok Adalat / Consumer Protection remedies for damages

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Overriding effect of the Act does not oust Lok Adalat / Consumer Protection remedies for damages
cases.holding: Section 174 gives the Act overriding effect only for matters provided under it; Section 50 does not empower the Supply Code to ascertain damages for a licensee's wrongful acts, and the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (Para 7.10, Clauses 7.7.1-7.7.5) covers only supply-related matters, not tortious damages for illegal disconnection. The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is preserved (ss.173/174), and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (Lok Adalat) is a special Act for such damages; the Lok Adalat therefore had jurisdiction, to which the petitioners had in any event submitted.

EA2003::2(15).code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.2(15), 'consumer'; s.2(20), 'electric line'; s.2(77), 'works') read with s.135
EA2003::2(15).clause: s.2(15) 'consumer' definition — second limb ('premises connected with works for receiving electricity') vis-a-vis owner's liability for theft detected at leased-out premises
EA2003::2(15).topic: An owner of premises where theft of electricity is detected can be held liable for assessment purposes as a 'consumer' under s.2(15), even where he claims the premises was let out, since the premises' 'works' being connected for receiving electricity suffices — lack of mens rea (relevant to criminal liability under s.135) does not exempt the owner from civil assessment liability, particularly where an unsubstantiated leasing claim caused revenue loss

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: An owner of premises where theft of electricity is detected can be held liable for assessment purposes as a 'consumer' under s.2(15), even where he claims the premises was let out, since the premises' 'works' being connected for receiving electricity suffices — lack of mens rea (relevant to criminal liability under s.135) does not exempt the owner from civil assessment liability, particularly where an unsubstantiated leasing claim caused revenue loss
cases.holding: Yes. Section 135's widest-possible scope (using 'whoever', 'person', 'consumer', 'occupant' interchangeably) shows the legislature did not confine its mischief by any hyper-technical plea as to individual status. The s.2(15) 'consumer' definition's second limb covers any person whose premises are for the time being connected with the works (electric line, transformer, apparatus) of a licensee 'for the purpose of receiving electricity', without requiring a contractual/supply relationship — this is broad enough to include an owner. A bare, unsubstantiated claim of having let out the premises (disbelieved by both the Assessing Officer and Appellate Authority, and not substantiated before the High Court either) does not exempt the owner from assessment liability, though it may bear on the separate criminal-law mens rea requirement under s.135. On the facts, the petitioner did not dispute ownership and did not challenge the theft allegation or quantum in his objections — only bare non-occupancy was pleaded and disbelieved.

EA2003::42.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with UPERC CGRF & Ombudsman Regulations, 2007)
EA2003::42.topic: CGRF/Ombudsman cannot relegate a consumer's dispute to arbitration

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.topic: CGRF/Ombudsman cannot relegate a consumer's dispute to arbitration
cases.holding: No. Under Section 42(5)-(8) and the Regulations, 2007, the ECGRF and Ombudsman are under a statutory duty to decide a consumer's grievance on merits; an arbitration clause in the agreement is at most an additional forum (Section 42(8) — without prejudice to other rights; right of election) and does not oust the statutory forum. The special statute overrides the general Arbitration Act. Regulation 5.1 bars the Forum only from matters under ss.126, 127, 128, 135-139, 143, 152 and 161; other disputes (Reg. 5.2) it must decide. The ECGRF erred in diverting the dispute to arbitration.
cases.flag: Maintainability: a writ by the Executive Engineer alone (an officer, not a juristic person) without the Distribution Licensee (PVVNL) was held not maintainable, but the Court decided on merits anyway (paras 62-63).

cases.title: Kisan Cold Storage & Ice Factory v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. (Full Bench reference)
cases.topic: Only a consumer, not the Distribution Licensee, may approach the Electricity Ombudsman; Regulation 8.1(i) is ultra vires to the extent it includes the licensee
cases.holding: No. Section 42(5) constitutes the Forum for redressal of consumer grievances; Section 42(6) gives only a 'consumer' aggrieved by non-redressal the right to represent to the Ombudsman; Section 42(7) requires the Ombudsman to settle 'the grievance of the consumer'. The Act and Rule 7 of the Electricity Rules, 2005 nowhere contemplate a grievance-redressal remedy for the Distribution Licensee. Regulation 8.1(i) of the 2007 Regulations, in extending the Ombudsman remedy to the Distribution Licensee as well, is inconsistent with and therefore ultra vires Section 42(5)-(7) and Section 181(1) (regulations must be consistent with the Act); a statutory right of appeal/representation must be found in the statute itself, not manufactured by subordinate regulation.

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: A licensee has no remedy of representation before the Ombudsman against a CGRF order
cases.holding: The licensee has no remedy to file a representation under Clause 8 of the 2007 Regulations read with Section 42(6) of the Act before the Ombudsman against an order of the CGRF, following Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Vidyut Lokpal, Lucknow (which struck down Clause 8 to that extent).

cases.title: Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission v. Reliance Energy Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Billing must follow actual meter readings; a Regulatory Commission cannot issue a blanket refund direction for supplementary/amended bills without a proper s.128 investigation, and individual consumer billing grievances go through the s.42(5) Forum/s.42(6) Ombudsman, not the Commission directly
cases.holding: (a) No — billing must be on the basis of actual meter reading; the licensee bears responsibility for meter maintenance/replacement, and any additional/amended billing must follow due statutory process, not an unexplained years-later reassessment on a presumed basis. (b) The Commission does have a general power under Section 128(6) to direct licensees to bring billing practices into conformity with the statute, but exercising that power via a blanket direction to refund all amounts collected — without first conducting an investigation and obtaining a report under Section 128(1)/(5) — exceeds its jurisdiction; and in any event the Commission's own adjudicatory function under Section 86(1)(f) is limited to licensee-generator disputes, not individual consumer grievances. The correct route for individual billing grievances is the Section 42(5) Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum, with a further remedy before the Section 42(6) Ombudsman. In substitution of the Commission's blanket refund order, the Court directed licensees to publish notice inviting affected consumers to make representations for redress (decided after a hearing), with a further remedy via ss.42(5)/(6) for those still dissatisfied.

EA2003::43.clause: s.43 (duty to supply); reconnection vs fresh connection
EA2003::43.topic: Duty to supply is not absolute; consumer-premises synergy; reconnection = same premises

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Duty to supply is not absolute; consumer-premises synergy; reconnection = same premises
cases.holding: The duty to supply under s.43 is not absolute and is subject to the charges and compliances stipulated by the utility as part of the application for supply; it is owed to the owner or occupier of particular premises, and one becomes a 'consumer' only with respect to those premises for which electricity is sought and provided. An application for the same premises for which supply was earlier provided is a 'reconnection'; different premises make it a fresh connection even if the consumer is the same.

EA2003::46.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (read with Clauses 4.6 & 4.21, Supply Code 2005)
EA2003::46.topic: Recoverable expenditure — actual expenses proved vs the licensee's own statutory obligation

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Recoverable expenditure — actual expenses proved vs the licensee's own statutory obligation
cases.holding: Under Section 46 a licensee may recover only “expenses reasonably incurred in providing any electric line or electrical plant”, and the burden to prove actual expenditure lies on the licensee (as the Supreme Court's remand directed). Extension of distribution mains and commissioning of new sub-stations is the licensee's own statutory obligation under the first proviso to Section 43(1) and cannot be loaded onto the consumer. On the evidence the 4-pole structure and service line were actually constructed, so Rs. 5,49,181 and Rs. 4,65,000 were rightly retained; the processing fee of Rs. 5,000 is non-refundable per the Cost Data Book.
cases.flag: The Supreme Court's remand order dated 29.11.2022 (in this very case) fixed the frame: refund is to be denied only “to the extent” the respondents prove “the actual expenses incurred.”

EA2003::47.clause: s.47(1) ('subject to the provisions of this section')
EA2003::47.topic: 'Subject to the provisions of this section' in s.47(1) means s.47 read as a whole, not subservient to sub-section (5) alone

cases.title: M/S Dev Prayag Paper Mill (Pvt.) & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors. (batch of ~90 connected writ petitions)
cases.topic: 'Subject to the provisions of this section' in s.47(1) means s.47 read as a whole, not subservient to sub-section (5) alone
cases.holding: The words 'subject to the provisions of this section' in Section 47(1) indicate that the fixation of reasonable security is governed by Section 47 read as a whole; sub-sections (1) and (2) are not made subject to sub-section (5) alone, rejecting the petitioners' submission (relying on the Black's Law Dictionary meaning of 'subject to' as explained in Saurashtra Chemicals) that sub-section (5) overrides sub-sections (1)-(4).

EA2003::56.topic: Recovery by suit is independent of the disconnection power

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Recovery by suit is independent of the disconnection power
cases.holding: The power to initiate recovery proceedings by filing a suit against a defaulting consumer is independent of the power to disconnect supply as a means of recovery under Section 56.

cases.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: For assessed dues, the sum 'first becomes due' under s.56(2) only on final assessment, not on the date of provisional assessment or the underlying checking/inspection
cases.holding: No — under s.126, a sum cannot be held 'due' against a consumer until the final assessment is made (here, 21.6.2013); the recovery citation issued 19.11.2013 was therefore well within two years of the sum first becoming due, and s.56(2) was not attracted.

cases.title: Shyam Ferrous Ltd. Gopal Nagar v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.topic: The s.56(2)/Clause 6.15 two-year recovery bar applies only prospectively, to liabilities arising after the Electricity Act, 2003 came into force; liabilities from the pre-2003 regime (here, 2002 peak-hour-restriction violations) are governed by the earlier law (s.24, 1910 Act) which imposes no such limitation on the power to demand/recover, per s.6 of the General Clauses Act preserving accrued liabilities on repeal
cases.holding: No. Section 56(2) applies only after the Electricity Act, 2003 came into force; liabilities incurred under the pre-2003 regime continue to be governed by s.24 of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (which imposes no limitation on the licensee's power to demand/recover, only providing a separate, non-exclusive suit remedy) by virtue of s.6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which preserves rights/liabilities accrued under a repealed enactment — following Kusumam Hotels (P) Ltd. v. Kerala SEB. Electricity Supply Code 2002's Clause 6.31.2 (an analogue to Clause 6.15) similarly bars only recovery via the 1958 Dues Recovery Act route after two years from when a sum 'first became due' — and a sum 'first becomes due,' for this purpose, only when a proper bill is raised and remains unpaid, not from the date of the underlying default (following MCD v. H.D. Shourie and NDMC v. Karam Chandra Thapar). Here, the correct penalty (per the Supreme Court's 25.7.2006 formula in U.P. Power Corp. v. Lohia Brass) was billed for the first time on 4.2.2009, with follow-up notices in 2009, and recovery proceedings under the 1958 Act commenced well within any two-year window measured from that billing — the intervening 13 years since the 2002 violations reflects an earlier (unauthorised, later-corrected) waiver by a Deputy General Manager lacking power to grant it, not licensee inaction after proper billing. Service of the demand notices by registered post to the recorded address was deemed sufficient under Explanation 1 to s.3 of the 1958 Act, notwithstanding the petitioner's claimed non-receipt (particularly given the petitioner's own subsequent conduct — seeking temporary reconnection, earlier partial payment under protest — evidencing awareness of the liability). Writ petition dismissed, with six months allowed for deposit and recovery held in abeyance meanwhile.

EA2003::56(2).topic: Limitation on recovery — recurring companion provision in Supply Code litigation

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Limitation on recovery — recurring companion provision in Supply Code litigation
cases.holding: "Sum due" means an amount adjudicated between the parties; un-adjudicated, escalating demands raised years after the service ended are barred.
cases.flag: Respondent pleaded this as "Clause 56(2) of the U.P. Supply Code"; the provision quoted and applied is s.56(2) of the Act. Recorded, not merged.

cases.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Rahamatullah Khan alias Rahamjulla
cases.topic: Meaning of 'first due'; disconnection barred after two years but recovery not
cases.holding: 'First due' means when the bill is first issued (the liability arises on consumption but the sum becomes due only on billing). Section 56(2) bars only the remedy of disconnection after two years from the sum first becoming due (unless continuously shown as arrears); it does not bar a supplementary/additional demand or other modes of recovery. In a case of bona fide mistake, limitation for the additional demand runs from discovery (s.17(1)(c), Limitation Act, 1963), but the licensee still cannot disconnect supply — only pursue other recovery.

EA2003::64.topic: Truing up cannot change the methodology of the original tariff determination

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.topic: Truing up cannot change the methodology of the original tariff determination
cases.holding: No. A tariff order under s.64 is quasi-judicial and binding until amended/revoked under s.64(6); truing up is only the adjustment of actuals against projections and cannot be used to re-think de novo the basic principles or retrospectively change the methodology of the initial determination. The DERC's changes on Issues 1, 2, 3 and 5 (LPSC/collection efficiency, depreciation, FR/SR salary, fringe benefit tax) were impermissible and are set aside; interest on Consumer Security Deposit (Issue 4) is a legitimate expense the appellants may recover.

JH-2005::9.2.code: Jharkhand SERC (Electricity Supply Code) Regulations, 2005 (framed under s.50, EA 2003)
JH-2005::9.2.topic: Reduction of contract demand — the 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement

cases.title: Jharkhand State Electricity Board & Others v. M/s Ramkrishna Forging Limited
cases.topic: Reduction of contract demand — the 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement
cases.holding: The initial agreement. Enhancement 'fresh agreements' for the same connection are merely supplementary amendments of the initial agreement (contract demand can be varied even by written communication, Reg. 2(l); reduction itself is by supplementary agreement, Reg. 9.2.6). So the three-year 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement (2004), not the last enhancement (2007); the 2007 reduction application was beyond it and is deemed allowed under Reg. 9.2. The Regulations are liberally construed for the consumer.

OFFTOPIC::abuse-of-process-departmental-.code: General (abuse of the writ process; supervisory direction)
OFFTOPIC::abuse-of-process-departmental-.clause: direction for departmental inquiry into collusive non-recovery
OFFTOPIC::abuse-of-process-departmental-.topic: Nine-year evasion of a lawful assessment, including grant of a fresh connection without full payment, warranted a departmental inquiry

cases.title: M/S Hind Industries Limited v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Nine-year evasion of a lawful assessment, including grant of a fresh connection without full payment, warranted a departmental inquiry
cases.holding: Where the record showed apparent collusion between the consumer and the licensee's officers — a modification application concealed as 'pending' when it had in fact been decided over a year earlier, and a fresh connection released to a nine-year defaulter on a bank guarantee rather than full payment — the Court, while dismissing the writ petition as an abuse of process, directed the Principal Secretary (Energy) to hold a detailed inquiry into the officers' and the petitioner's conduct and take consequential action against those responsible.

OFFTOPIC::aptel-jurisdiction-over-cerc-r.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.79, 111, 121, 178) — APTEL's appellate jurisdiction vis-a-vis CERC's delegated regulation-making power
OFFTOPIC::aptel-jurisdiction-over-cerc-r.clause: s.111 (appeal to APTEL) vis-a-vis s.178 (CERC's power to make Regulations) and s.121 (APTEL's general powers)
OFFTOPIC::aptel-jurisdiction-over-cerc-r.topic: APTEL has no jurisdiction under s.111 to decide the vires of CERC Regulations made under s.178 (a delegated-legislation function reviewable only via Article 226); s.121 does not confer judicial-review power on APTEL; CERC was empowered under the residuary s.178(1)/(2)(ze) to cap electricity-trading margins by Regulation

cases.title: PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, thr. Secy. (and connected appeals)
cases.topic: APTEL has no jurisdiction under s.111 to decide the vires of CERC Regulations made under s.178 (a delegated-legislation function reviewable only via Article 226); s.121 does not confer judicial-review power on APTEL; CERC was empowered under the residuary s.178(1)/(2)(ze) to cap electricity-trading margins by Regulation
cases.holding: (i) Section 178 (CERC's regulation-making power) is wider than the enumerated Order/decision-making functions under s.79(1). (ii) A s.178 Regulation, as delegated legislation, intervenes in and can override existing contracts between regulated entities. (iii) Because a s.178 Regulation is delegated legislation, its validity can be tested only by judicial review before the courts (Article 226), not by appeal to APTEL under s.111. (iv) Section 121 does not confer a power of judicial review on APTEL — the words 'orders', 'instructions', or 'directions' therein do not extend to invalidating subordinate legislation. (v) Where a dispute concerns the interpretation (not the validity) of a s.178 Regulation, an appeal lies to APTEL under s.111, but no appeal lies on the Regulation's validity. (vi) Applying the 'generality versus enumeration' principle, CERC was empowered, under the residuary s.178(1) read with s.178(2)(ze), to cap trading margins in inter-State electricity trading by Regulation. The reference was accordingly answered: APTEL has no jurisdiction to decide the validity of CERC Regulations framed under s.178; such validity may only be challenged by judicial review under Article 226. All appeals dismissed.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~3670 lines) and its subject (APTEL/CERC regulatory-jurisdiction architecture for inter-State electricity trading), which is distinct from the U.P. Electricity Supply Code's retail billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::criminal-interim.topic: Interlocutory stay in a s.482 complaint-quashing petition

cases.title: Dr. Vinod Kumar Bassi v. The State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Interlocutory stay in a s.482 complaint-quashing petition
cases.holding: On the applicant's contention that the complaint was proceeded with without the Section 202(1) Cr.P.C. enquiry (applicant residing in Lucknow, complaint filed in Hardoi), notice was ordered and further proceedings stayed till the next date. No merits were decided.
cases.flag: Off-topic for the Supply Code: a two-line interlocutory criminal order under Section 482 Cr.P.C.; no Electricity Supply Code provision is involved. Retained only for queue completeness.

OFFTOPIC::cross-subsidy-surcharge-sez-de.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.14(b), 42) & Special Economic Zone Act, 2005 (s.49) — CSS/open-access wholesale regime, not the retail Supply Code
OFFTOPIC::cross-subsidy-surcharge-sez-de.clause: s.14(b) deemed-licensee proviso vis-a-vis 'consumer' status and CSS liability
OFFTOPIC::cross-subsidy-surcharge-sez-de.topic: A single-unit SEZ developer deemed a distribution licensee under s.14(b) remains liable, as a 'consumer', to pay Cross Subsidy Surcharge to the area distribution licensee when procuring its entire power for captive use from another generator

cases.title: M/S Sesa Sterlite Ltd. v. Orissa Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.topic: A single-unit SEZ developer deemed a distribution licensee under s.14(b) remains liable, as a 'consumer', to pay Cross Subsidy Surcharge to the area distribution licensee when procuring its entire power for captive use from another generator
cases.holding: The deeming fiction in the proviso to Section 14(b) (SEZ developer = deemed distribution licensee) presupposes actual distribution of power to others; it cannot be stretched to exempt a developer who establishes an SEZ solely for its own single unit and consumes the entire power itself, from CSS liability as a 'consumer' under Section 2(15). CSS compensates the area distribution licensee for the loss of cross-subsidy revenue when a consumer situated in its area procures power from elsewhere via open access, regardless of whether the licensee's own line is physically used, and applies whether or not the deemed-licensee status is held. The appellant's transmission line was found (on the facts) not to be a 'dedicated transmission line' exempting it from this liability. The appeal was dismissed.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale and its subject (CSS/open-access/SEZ interplay), which is distinct from the U.P. Electricity Supply Code billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::delay-and-laches-writ-jurisdic.clause: delay and laches bar equitable relief even for similarly-situated claimants
OFFTOPIC::delay-and-laches-writ-jurisdic.topic: A consumer who did not timely challenge withdrawal of a benefit cannot invoke a later favourable judgment obtained by other litigants more than two decades afterward

cases.title: M/S Three Star Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 5 Ors.
cases.topic: A consumer who did not timely challenge withdrawal of a benefit cannot invoke a later favourable judgment obtained by other litigants more than two decades afterward
cases.holding: Those who were vigilant and raised their dispute in time are entitled to the benefit of a subsequent favourable judgment (here, Pawan Alloys, 1997, on promissory estoppel for a development rebate); a consumer who accepted withdrawal of the rebate without protest, and made no claim until a year after the judgment (1998) and pursued it in this writ only decades later, is guilty of extraordinary delay and laches disentitling equitable relief under Article 226, irrespective of being similarly situated to successful litigants.

OFFTOPIC::discom-unbundling-employee-pen.code: Delhi Electric Reforms Act, 2000 (ss.14-16, 57) and Delhi Electricity Reforms (Transfer Scheme) Rules, 2001 (Rules 3, 6, 8) — successor-DISCOM liability for erstwhile Board employees' pension/terminal benefits
OFFTOPIC::discom-unbundling-employee-pen.clause: Rule 6(8)/(9) (personnel-related liability transfer) and Rule 8(3) (litigation-liability cap) of the Transfer Scheme Rules, 2001
OFFTOPIC::discom-unbundling-employee-pen.topic: Successor DISCOM liability for pension/terminal-benefit claims of Delhi Vidyut Board employees who had already retired/been dismissed before unbundling — an employer-succession dispute among privatised distribution companies, unrelated to consumer billing/Supply Code

cases.title: North Delhi Power Ltd. v. Govt. of N.C.T. of Delhi & Ors. (with BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Govt. of N.C.T. of Delhi & Anr.)
cases.topic: Successor DISCOM liability for pension/terminal-benefit claims of Delhi Vidyut Board employees who had already retired/been dismissed before unbundling — an employer-succession dispute among privatised distribution companies, unrelated to consumer billing/Supply Code
cases.holding: Rule 6 of the Transfer Scheme Rules, 2001 is a complete, self-contained code governing 'personnel and personnel-related matters' (Rule 3(2)), broad enough to cover retired, dismissed, and deceased employees, not merely those formally on the transfer list; under Rule 6(8), the relevant successor DISCOM stands substituted for the Board for all statutory/employment-related schemes including pension and superannuation funds for 'existing pensioners'. The litigation-liability cap in Rule 8(3) (Rs. 1 crore per annum per DISCOM) applies equally to personnel-related claims, not only third-party/consumer litigation. The successor DISCOMs (NDPL, BSES Rajdhani) were accordingly held liable for the pension/terminal-benefit claims of pre-unbundling retirees/dismissed employees of the erstwhile DVB, subject to the Rule 8(3) cap.
cases.paras: paras 15-56 (~209-para judgment; core reasoning at paras 15-33, 44-51)
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~2000 lines) and its subject (post-privatisation employer-successor pension/personnel liability dispute among DISCOMs), which has no nexus to the U.P. Electricity Supply Code's consumer billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::distribution-licensing-minimum.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.9, 10, 14, 15, 19, 42(2)) and Distribution of Electricity (Additional Requirement of Capital Adequacy...) Rules, 2005
OFFTOPIC::distribution-licensing-minimum.clause: ss.9/10 (captive plant vs generating company); Explanation to Rule 3 (minimum area of supply); s.19 (revocation); s.142 (penalty/natural justice)
OFFTOPIC::distribution-licensing-minimum.topic: Distribution licence grant/cancellation; minimum-area Explanation is a guideline, not a rigid bar, on these unusual facts; penalty requires a hearing

cases.title: M/S Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors. (with connected appeals)
cases.neutral_citation: Civil Appeal Nos. 3607-3610 of 2008, with C.A. Nos. 4104-4107 of 2008
cases.topic: Distribution licence grant/cancellation; minimum-area Explanation is a guideline, not a rigid bar, on these unusual facts; penalty requires a hearing
cases.holding: The Supreme Court restored a distribution licence earlier granted to JSPL (a captive-power-plant owner, governed by s.9 not s.10 of the Act) to supply a private industrial estate it had itself developed under a State Government MoU/permission predating the 2003 Act's full commencement and the 2005 Rules. The Appellate Tribunal had wrongly treated the Explanation to Rule 3 (minimum area of supply = a municipal area or revenue district) as an inflexible bar to a second/parallel licence in a smaller area; the Court held the historical background — investment made, the State's own power shortage, CSEB's admitted inability to supply the area, and long-term supply contracts already in place before the Rules existed — justified treating the case as an exception, and estoppel/vested-rights principles militated against retrospectively invalidating the licence. Separately, the Commission's Rs. 1 lakh penalty under s.142 for supplying without a licence was rightly set aside by the Tribunal for want of a hearing, since the licensing proceeding itself never framed the question of JSPL's liability to penalty.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~57 pages) and its subject (distribution licensing, not Supply Code billing/assessment/disconnection); not exhaustively digested. General electricity-law background only.

OFFTOPIC::dowry-death-bail-application.topic: Bail application in a dowry-death case under IPC ss.304-B/498-A and Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3/4 — no Supply Code nexus

cases.title: Mukesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: Bail application in a dowry-death case under IPC ss.304-B/498-A and Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3/4 — no Supply Code nexus
cases.holding: Bail granted with standard conditions (undertaking not to seek adjournments, presence at trial, compliance with proclamation/charge-framing/s.313 statement stages), given a co-accused's earlier bail and only general dowry-demand allegations against the applicant.
cases.flag: Recorded for completeness of the source corpus only; no jurisprudential content relevant to the Supply Code.

OFFTOPIC::dowry-death-criminal-appeal.topic: Criminal appeal against conviction under IPC ss.498-A/304-B and Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3/4 — no Supply Code nexus

cases.title: Maniram v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: Criminal appeal against conviction under IPC ss.498-A/304-B and Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3/4 — no Supply Code nexus
cases.holding: The Court set aside the s.304-B conviction for want of proximate-in-time cruelty evidence ('soon before her death'), citing Satvir Singh v. State of Punjab, Hira Lal v. State (NCT of Delhi), and Mustafa Shahadal Shaikh v. State of Maharashtra, while maintaining the convictions under s.498-A IPC and ss.3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, modifying sentences for two of the three appellants.
cases.flag: Recorded for completeness of the source corpus only; no jurisprudential content relevant to the Supply Code.

OFFTOPIC::electricity-board-employee-pub.code: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (s.2(1)(c)) vis-a-vis Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 (s.81) and IPC s.21
OFFTOPIC::electricity-board-employee-pub.clause: s.2(1)(c)(iii), 1988 Act (public servant) vis-a-vis s.81, 1948 Act (deemed public servant under IPC s.21)
OFFTOPIC::electricity-board-employee-pub.topic: An Electricity Board employee is a 'public servant' under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 independently of the 1948 Act's IPC-specific deeming provision, since the Board is a statutory corporation within s.2(1)(c)(iii) of the 1988 Act

cases.title: Naresh Kumar Madan v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.topic: An Electricity Board employee is a 'public servant' under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 independently of the 1948 Act's IPC-specific deeming provision, since the Board is a statutory corporation within s.2(1)(c)(iii) of the 1988 Act
cases.holding: A term defined in one statute cannot be construed solely by reference to its definition in a different statute; s.81 of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 deems Board employees 'public servants' only for purposes of s.21 IPC, but that does not exhaust the question of their status under the differently-and-more-broadly-worded 'public servant' definition in s.2(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, which independently captures any person in the service or pay of a corporation established by or under a Central, Provincial or State Act. The appellant, a Board employee, therefore answered the description of 'public servant' under the 1988 Act, and his prosecution for taking illegal gratification in connection with grant of an electrical connection was maintainable. The single-judge decision in Bimal Kumar Gupta v. Special Police Establishment Lokayukt holding otherwise was overruled as not laying down the correct law.
cases.flag: Recorded for corpus completeness; concerns the criminal-law 'public servant' status of Electricity Board employees for anti-corruption prosecution, not the Supply Code's consumer-facing billing/assessment/disconnection framework.

OFFTOPIC::electricity-duty-taxation.code: U.P. Electricity Duty Act, 1952 (s.3(2)) and notification dated 13.9.2012 (unrelated to the Electricity Act, 2003/Supply Code)
OFFTOPIC::electricity-duty-taxation.clause: s.3(2), 1952 Act; Entry 53, List II, Seventh Schedule

cases.topic: Validity of electricity duty on 'rate of charge' (including demand charge) under the U.P. Electricity Duty Act, 1952
cases.holding: The Court rejected the challenge to the notification dated 13.9.2012 levying electricity duty on the 'rate of charge' (including demand charges, not merely energy/consumption charges) and to the vires of Section 3(2) of the U.P. Electricity Duty Act, 1952 against Entry 53, List II of the Seventh Schedule; all ~85 connected writ petitions were dismissed.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~5450 lines / ~85 connected petitioners) and its subject (electricity duty taxation under a separate 1952 Act, not the Electricity Act, 2003/Supply Code billing-assessment-disconnection framework); not exhaustively digested.

cases.topic: Bare adjournment order with no substantive content

OFFTOPIC::family-pension-dispute.topic: Family pension dispute between two wives of a deceased municipal employee — no Supply Code content; cites electricity-board pension cases only as general persuasive analogues

cases.title: Manno Singh v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Family pension dispute between two wives of a deceased municipal employee — no Supply Code content; cites electricity-board pension cases only as general persuasive analogues
cases.holding: The second marriage, contracted after the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 came into force, was null and void; the second wife does not fall within the definition of 'family' under Regulation 2(f), and a nomination in her favour cannot defeat the legally wedded first wife's entitlement to family pension under Regulation 7.
cases.flag: Recorded for completeness of the source corpus; cites electricity-board pension precedents (Shakuntala Devi, Poonam Devi) only as general analogues, not for any Supply Code holding — no Electricity Act/Supply Code provision is engaged.

OFFTOPIC::government-servant-suspension-.code: U.P. Government Servant (Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1999 (Rule 4) — suspension pending disciplinary inquiry; incidental reference to U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 4.6(e), supervision charges)
OFFTOPIC::government-servant-suspension-.clause: Rule 4 (suspension requires application of mind to gravity of allegations) — Clause 4.6(e) (supervision charges payable to licensee before work begins) cited only as a factual defense
OFFTOPIC::government-servant-suspension-.topic: Suspension of a Development Authority engineer for alleged financial irregularity in an electric-line-shifting project quashed for want of application of mind; Clause 4.6(e) of the Supply Code (supervision charges due before work commencement) was invoked only to show the petitioner's processing of such charges was procedurally correct, not to establish any independent Supply Code holding

cases.title: Shabih Haider v. State of U.P. thru. Prin. Secy., Housing & Urban Planning & Ors.
cases.topic: Suspension of a Development Authority engineer for alleged financial irregularity in an electric-line-shifting project quashed for want of application of mind; Clause 4.6(e) of the Supply Code (supervision charges due before work commencement) was invoked only to show the petitioner's processing of such charges was procedurally correct, not to establish any independent Supply Code holding
cases.holding: The suspension order was quashed as passed without application of mind to Rule 4's requirement that suspension be resorted to only where allegations, if established, would warrant a major penalty; the record showed the petitioner had no substantive role in project conception, tender approval, or contract award, and had merely forwarded files in the ordinary course. On the specific supervision-charges allegation, the respondents conceded that Clause 4.6(e) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 requires such charges to be deposited with the licensee before commencement of work — meaning the charge that the petitioner had improperly processed centage payment 'prior to commencement of work' was, on the correct reading of Clause 4.6(e), based on a mistaken premise.
cases.flag: Recorded for completeness of the source corpus; the operative holding is a service-law suspension ruling, with Clause 4.6(e) of the Supply Code invoked only incidentally as a factual defense regarding timing of a supervision-charge payment — not itself a substantive Supply Code determination relevant to this project's consumer-facing focus.

OFFTOPIC::impossibility-billing-on-outsi.code: General maxim (lex non cogit ad impossibilia) applied to billing where the consumer's own meter cannot yield a reading
OFFTOPIC::impossibility-billing-on-outsi.clause: exceptional reliance on an outside/check meter for billing
OFFTOPIC::impossibility-billing-on-outsi.topic: Where the consumer's own meter is physically incapable of providing a reading, an independent check meter outside the premises may exceptionally found billing, if reliably maintained

cases.title: M/S Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Anr. v. PVVNL & Ors.
cases.topic: Where the consumer's own meter is physically incapable of providing a reading, an independent check meter outside the premises may exceptionally found billing, if reliably maintained
cases.holding: No statutory provision permits billing/assessment based on a meter other than the one installed at the consumer's premises; ordinarily the answer must go against the licensee for want of such a provision. However, the law does not require compliance with the impossible: where the consumer's own meter is destroyed (e.g. by fire) or stolen and cannot yield a reading, an independent/check meter installed by the licensee outside the premises may exceptionally be relied upon for billing, provided it is shown to be reliably and authentically maintained with the consumer's knowledge — applying lex non cogit ad impossibilia, impotentia excusat legem and nemo tenetur ad impossibilia, following the Division Bench in Inter College Kusmaul, Gorakhpur v. State of U.P.

OFFTOPIC::interim-relief-after-withdrawa.code: Constitutional/writ procedure (Article 226) — power to grant interim relief after a petition is dismissed as withdrawn
OFFTOPIC::interim-relief-after-withdrawa.topic: A writ court has no jurisdiction to grant interim protection for the interregnum once a petition is dismissed as withdrawn or the party is relegated to another forum, since Article 226 interim relief is only ancillary to a final relief obtainable on merits in a proceeding still pending before that court

cases.title: Om Prakash s/o Gauri Shankar v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: A writ court has no jurisdiction to grant interim protection for the interregnum once a petition is dismissed as withdrawn or the party is relegated to another forum, since Article 226 interim relief is only ancillary to a final relief obtainable on merits in a proceeding still pending before that court
cases.holding: Following the Constitution Bench in State of Orissa v. Madan Gopal Rungta (and its consistent subsequent approval), the Court held it lacks jurisdiction to grant interim relief (such as a stay of recovery) for the period during which a petitioner intends to approach the Clause-based Supply Code authority, once the writ petition itself has been dismissed as withdrawn; interim relief under Article 226 can only be granted as ancillary to final relief in a matter still pending before the court on merits.
cases.flag: General writ-jurisdiction/interim-relief principle applied in an electricity-recovery context; not itself a Supply Code holding, but the Supply Code recovery notice was the underlying dispute in which it arose.

OFFTOPIC::ipc-405-406-entrustment.code: Indian Penal Code, 1860 / Cr.P.C., 1973 (unrelated to the Electricity Act/Supply Code)
OFFTOPIC::ipc-405-406-entrustment.topic: Criminal breach of trust — commercial sale is not 'entrustment'; mandatory Section 202(1) enquiry

cases.title: Kishore Biyani v. State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Criminal breach of trust — commercial sale is not 'entrustment'; mandatory Section 202(1) enquiry
cases.holding: A mere commercial sale transaction (unpaid supply of goods) does not amount to 'entrustment' of property under Section 405 IPC; absent entrustment and dishonest misappropriation, no offence under Section 406 is made out. Where the accused resides outside the trial court's jurisdiction, Section 202(1) Cr.P.C. mandates an enquiry before summoning, and its omission vitiates the summoning order.
cases.flag: Entirely off-topic to the Supply Code jurisprudence; recorded only to keep the source-corpus review complete. No provision-holdings or authorities from this case are added to the Supply Code index.

OFFTOPIC::jurisdiction-not-by-consent.clause: no jurisdiction by consent, acquiescence, or waiver
OFFTOPIC::jurisdiction-not-by-consent.topic: Jurisdiction of a tribunal of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or an unreasoned prior order

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: Jurisdiction of a tribunal of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or an unreasoned prior order
