cases.holding: A tribunal or forum of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot derive jurisdiction beyond the statute; no acquiescence, consent, or waiver can confer it, and a defect of jurisdiction cannot be cured even by consent, rendering any resulting order a nullity.

OFFTOPIC::landlord-tenant-civil.clause: Article 227; interim injunction to restore supply
OFFTOPIC::landlord-tenant-civil.topic: Restoration of a tenant's electric supply by civil injunction

cases.title: Dipali Dey (Baxi) v. Mira Das
cases.topic: Restoration of a tenant's electric supply by civil injunction
cases.holding: Where a tenant in possession has had supply disconnected by the landlord, the civil court may by injunction direct restoration pending the tenancy suit; the High Court should not interfere with such concurrent orders under Article 227. The tenancy dispute abides the trial.
cases.flag: Off-topic for the Supply Code: a Supreme Court order on a landlord-tenant civil injunction to restore supply; no Electricity Supply Code provision is construed. Retained as a node in the landlord-tenant disconnection line (cf. SCJ-016, SCJ-020).

OFFTOPIC::lps-change-in-law-ppa.code: Power Purchase Agreements (contractual Change-in-Law and Late Payment Surcharge clauses) — bulk generation procurement, unrelated to the retail Supply Code
OFFTOPIC::lps-change-in-law-ppa.clause: Change-in-Law clause vis-a-vis RBI PLR-to-Base-Rate/MCLR transition
OFFTOPIC::lps-change-in-law-ppa.topic: RBI's replacement of PLR with Base Rate/MCLR did not entitle the distribution company to recompute LPS at the new (lower) rate, given concurrent factual findings and the company's own prior acceptance of invoices

cases.title: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.topic: RBI's replacement of PLR with Base Rate/MCLR did not entitle the distribution company to recompute LPS at the new (lower) rate, given concurrent factual findings and the company's own prior acceptance of invoices
cases.holding: The Supreme Court declined to disturb the concurrent findings of MERC and APTEL rejecting the distribution company's claim that the RBI's introduction of the Base Rate (2010) and MCLR (2016) systems, replacing the PLR methodology, constituted a 'Change in Law' under the Power Purchase Agreements entitling it to pay Late Payment Surcharge at the lower Base Rate/MCLR-linked rate instead of the PLR-based SBAR rate defined in the agreements; the distribution company had accepted and reconciled the invoiced LPS without dispute for years, and could not introduce fresh material in a second appeal under Section 125 not tendered before the regulatory authorities below.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~5170 lines) and its subject (bulk power-procurement PPA/LPS contract dispute), which is distinct from the U.P. Electricity Supply Code billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::mala-fide-impleadment.clause: plea of mala fide requires eo nomine impleadment
OFFTOPIC::mala-fide-impleadment.topic: A plea of mala fide cannot be entertained unless the official against whom it is alleged is impleaded eo nomine

cases.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: A plea of mala fide cannot be entertained unless the official against whom it is alleged is impleaded eo nomine
cases.holding: It is settled law that a plea of mala fide/bias against a named official cannot be entertained unless that official is impleaded eo nomine and given an opportunity to meet the allegation; the petitioner's mala fide plea failed for want of such impleadment.

OFFTOPIC::precedent-jindal-poly-films.clause: overruling a Division Bench decision that did not engage the specific statutory provision

cases.title: Kisan Cold Storage & Ice Factory v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. (Full Bench reference)
cases.topic: Jindal Poly Films Ltd. overruled
cases.holding: The Division Bench in Jindal Poly Films Ltd. v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission (15.4.2011) upheld Regulation 8.1(i) as intra vires on a general assertion that the Act should be read as a whole rather than section by section, without specifically engaging Section 42(5)-(7); that reasoning does not lay down the correct principle of law and is overruled.

cases.title: Gaya Prasad v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Empty listing order
cases.holding: At the petitioner's request the case was passed over for the day and listed in the next cause list; nothing was decided.
cases.flag: No substantive content: a bare pass-over/listing order with no Supply Code (or any) determination. Retained only for queue completeness.

OFFTOPIC::rerc-open-access-regulations-v.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.9, 42, 79(1)(c), 86(1)(c), 178, 181) — CERC/State Commission jurisdictional demarcation over open access; Rajasthan Open Access Regulations, 2016 (Regulations 21, 26(7))
OFFTOPIC::rerc-open-access-regulations-v.clause: ss.42/86(1)(c)/181 (State Commission's intra-state open-access jurisdiction) vis-a-vis s.79(1)(c) (CERC's inter-state transmission jurisdiction)
OFFTOPIC::rerc-open-access-regulations-v.topic: State Electricity Regulatory Commissions retain jurisdiction to regulate the intra-state aspects of open access (including deviation penalties and advance-scheduling requirements for captive power plants and inter-state consumers) even where the power originates outside the state; such regulatory measures are not ultra vires or unreasonable restrictions on the statutory open-access right

cases.title: Ramayana Ispat Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. State of Rajasthan & Ors. (with connected appeals)
cases.topic: State Electricity Regulatory Commissions retain jurisdiction to regulate the intra-state aspects of open access (including deviation penalties and advance-scheduling requirements for captive power plants and inter-state consumers) even where the power originates outside the state; such regulatory measures are not ultra vires or unreasonable restrictions on the statutory open-access right
cases.holding: The Court held: (i) RERC had jurisdiction to regulate the intra-state aspects of open access transactions under ss.42(2)/(3), 86(1)(c) and 181 of the Act of 2003, notwithstanding that the power might originate from outside Rajasthan or that CERC has jurisdiction under s.79(1)(c) over inter-state transmission — the key determinant is delivery/consumption within the state's intra-state grid, not the power's source; (ii) penalties under Regulation 21 for deviation/under-injection by captive power plants are a legitimate, uniformly-applied grid-discipline measure serving the Act's objectives (preventing gaming, ensuring frequency stability), not a discriminatory or unreasonable restriction on the s.9(1) proviso right to captive generation; (iii) Regulation 26(7)'s 24-hour advance-notice requirement for short-term inter-state open access is a reasonable procedural safeguard for grid stability and scheduling discipline, not an ultra vires or arbitrary barrier to open access, particularly since real-time/day-ahead market alternatives remain available for urgent procurement; and (iv) courts must exercise judicial restraint and defer to specialized regulatory commissions' technical/economic determinations, interfering only where a regulation is shown to be wholly irrational, ultra vires the parent statute, or violative of fundamental rights. All three appeals were accordingly dismissed and the High Court judgments upholding the Regulations of 2016 affirmed.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~2755 lines) and its subject (CERC/State Commission open-access regulatory jurisdiction and captive-generation deviation penalties), which is distinct from the U.P. Electricity Supply Code's retail billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::s156-3-crpc-tree-felling-dispu.topic: Criminal revision against dismissal of a s.156(3) Cr.P.C. application over a forged-consent tree-felling dispute between land co-sharers — no Supply Code nexus

cases.title: Shiv Murti Yadav v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.topic: Criminal revision against dismissal of a s.156(3) Cr.P.C. application over a forged-consent tree-felling dispute between land co-sharers — no Supply Code nexus
cases.holding: The revisional court's jurisdiction is narrower than appellate jurisdiction, warranting interference only for gross error, non-compliance with law, unsupported findings, or perverse exercise of discretion; finding none of these, and noting the proper remedy for police inaction on an FIR is a complaint before the Magistrate (not a writ or revision), the revision was dismissed.
cases.flag: Recorded for completeness of the source corpus only; no jurisprudential content relevant to the Supply Code.

OFFTOPIC::s434-ipc-quashing-application.topic: s.482 Cr.P.C. application to quash a charge-sheet under s.434 IPC arising from an encroachment-demolition/extortion dispute — no Supply Code nexus

cases.title: Rakesh Kaushik v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.topic: s.482 Cr.P.C. application to quash a charge-sheet under s.434 IPC arising from an encroachment-demolition/extortion dispute — no Supply Code nexus
cases.holding: Notice issued to respondents with time for counter/rejoinder affidavits; interim protection granted restraining coercive action in the pending criminal case, without affecting separate encroachment-removal proceedings or permitting reconstruction of the demolished portion.
cases.flag: Recorded for completeness of the source corpus only; no jurisprudential content relevant to the Supply Code.

OFFTOPIC::s62-6-interest-generation-tari.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.62(6)) — wholesale generation-tariff dispute, unrelated to the retail Supply Code
OFFTOPIC::s62-6-interest-generation-tari.clause: s.62(6) construed narrowly: no interest on a provisional-vs-final tariff differential absent a specific regulation
OFFTOPIC::s62-6-interest-generation-tari.topic: Section 62(6) interest does not extend to the interim/provisional tariff period pending final determination, absent an express regulation; equity/restitution principles do not independently justify interest absent any statutory, contractual, or customary basis

cases.title: M/S NTPC Ltd. v. M.P. State Electricity Board & Ors. (with connected appeals)
cases.topic: Section 62(6) interest does not extend to the interim/provisional tariff period pending final determination, absent an express regulation; equity/restitution principles do not independently justify interest absent any statutory, contractual, or customary basis
cases.holding: Section 62(6) only prohibits recovery of a price 'exceeding the tariff determined under this section' — it does not address the interim period during which tariff determination is pending, nor deem a subsequently-reduced final tariff to retroactively convert prior lawful interim charges into 'excess' charges attracting interest. CERC's 2006 Regulation 5A (providing simple interest on provisional-vs-final tariff differentials) could not apply retrospectively to the 2001-2004 period in issue. The Appellate Tribunal erred in awarding interest on equity/justice/fair-play grounds, since there was no contractual, statutory, or regulatory basis for interest, no industry practice of paying it, and no finding that the generating company had coercively or unjustly extracted the interim tariff (which was charged strictly per the Commission's own continuing notifications).
cases.flag: SC's authoritative narrow construction of s.62(6) interest ('exceeding the tariff determined') — useful cross-reference for retail Supply Code cases construing the same provision (cf. SCJ-072 Kamla Cold Storage, which similarly held s.62(6) inapplicable to a delayed rebate).

OFFTOPIC::service-law-natural-justice.code: Service law / departmental inquiry (not the Supply Code)
OFFTOPIC::service-law-natural-justice.topic: Burden on the Establishment to prove charges in a major-penalty inquiry

cases.title: Dhirendra Kumar Chaudhary v. State of U.P. & 5 Others
cases.topic: Burden on the Establishment to prove charges in a major-penalty inquiry
cases.holding: In a departmental inquiry carrying a major penalty, the Establishment must prove the charges by leading documentary and oral evidence through a Presenting Officer, with witnesses offered for cross-examination, before an inquiry tribunal that distances itself from the Establishment; relying on mere complaints and considering material (further inquiry/I.T.-cell reports) behind the employee's back vitiates the proceedings for breach of natural justice. Dismissal quashed; reinstatement, with liberty to hold a fresh inquiry from the charge-sheet stage.
cases.flag: Off-topic for the Supply Code: this is a service/disciplinary matter. The Supply Code, 2005 appears only as the backdrop of the misconduct charge (irregular bill revisions); no Code provision is construed. Retained in the corpus for completeness (and for its authorities).

OFFTOPIC::transmission-scheme-siting-dis.code: Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 (ss.28, 29) — transmission scheme preparation, publication, and sanctioning
OFFTOPIC::transmission-scheme-siting-dis.clause: ss.28-29 (scheme preparation/publication/sanctioning) — validity challenge and re-alignment claim by a subsequent purchaser
OFFTOPIC::transmission-scheme-siting-dis.topic: A subsequent land purchaser who neither made nor inherited a timely representation against a validly-published transmission scheme cannot belatedly seek re-alignment of an already-substantially-executed scheme; parallel pursuit of a civil suit and writ petition for the same relief is an abuse of process

cases.title: Orissa Power Transmission Corporation Ltd. & Ors. v. Asian School of Business Management Trust & Ors.
cases.topic: A subsequent land purchaser who neither made nor inherited a timely representation against a validly-published transmission scheme cannot belatedly seek re-alignment of an already-substantially-executed scheme; parallel pursuit of a civil suit and writ petition for the same relief is an abuse of process
cases.holding: The scheme (notified 1991, modified 1996) was validly published under ss.28/29 with full technical details available for inspection as specified; since neither the original landowner nor the respondent trust (which purchased the land and built on it 14+ years after publication) made any representation within the statutory window, they had no locus to belatedly challenge the scheme or seek re-alignment after ~150 towers had already been erected at a cost of over Rs. 14 crore. The Division Bench of the High Court erred in ordering re-alignment, having overlooked that the respondent stepped into the shoes of a party with no grievance, and in applying a half-baked feasibility analysis over the appellants' unrebutted technical objections. Additionally, pursuing a civil suit for injunction in parallel with two successive writ petitions seeking substantially the same relief, and withdrawing the suit only once the writ appeal was entertained, constituted an abuse of process; the second writ petition should have been dismissed on this ground, distinguishing S.J.S. Business Enterprises (which involved a suit withdrawn early, not maintained in parallel through appeal).
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its subject (transmission-tower siting/land dispute under the wholesale infrastructure provisions of the 1948 Act), which has no nexus to the U.P. Electricity Supply Code's consumer billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

TORT::compensation-assessment.code: Law of torts / Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (guidance)
TORT::compensation-assessment.clause: restitutio in integram; MV Act multiplier method
TORT::compensation-assessment.topic: Assessment of damages for electrocution disability

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Assessment of damages for electrocution disability
cases.holding: Damages for loss of limb/life flow from tort principles (restitutio in integram); the Permanent Lok Adalat rightly took guidance from the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 second schedule / multiplier method to compute compensation for a 100% disability, and ~Rs. 21 lakh was not excessive. A departmental circular capping compensation at Rs. 2 lakh binds the Corporation's officials but not the court.

UP-2002::8.1.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code (interest on delayed dues, Clause 8.1)
UP-2002::8.1.topic: Interest on a delayed/evaded assessment is a necessary corollary of retention, neither penal nor confiscatory

cases.title: M/S Hind Industries Limited v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Interest on a delayed/evaded assessment is a necessary corollary of retention, neither penal nor confiscatory
cases.holding: Payment of interest on money retained for years (here at the Clause 8.1 rate of 16% compoundable every six months) is a necessary corollary of retention and is neither penal nor confiscatory (following Wig Brothers). The question of whether the 2003 Act (rather than pre-2003 dues) governed the applicable rate, and the exact rate, was left to the competent authority, but the Court directed that in the facts of the case interest could not be less than the bank rate applicable for the relevant period.

UP-2002::area-level-committee-jurisdicti.clause: jurisdiction over representations against assessment (Area Level Committee/CGM vs. Superintending Engineer/DGM)
UP-2002::area-level-committee-jurisdicti.topic: Representations against an assessment exceeding Rs. 10 lakh lie before the Area Level Committee, not the Superintending Engineer (whose jurisdiction was capped at Rs. 2 lakh)

cases.title: M/S Hind Industries Limited v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Representations against an assessment exceeding Rs. 10 lakh lie before the Area Level Committee, not the Superintending Engineer (whose jurisdiction was capped at Rs. 2 lakh)
cases.holding: The Area Level Committee/CGM had jurisdiction, since under the Code, 2002 the Committee at circle level/DGM (Superintending Engineer) could decide representations only up to Rs. 2 lakh, while representations concerning recoveries above Rs. 10 lakh had to be decided by the Committee at area level/CGM; a 2010 modification order accordingly directed the representation to the Area Level Committee instead. However, even accepting the petitioner's own contention that the Superintending Engineer lacked jurisdiction, this meant only that the representation itself had been filed before an incompetent authority and any order thereon was of no consequence — it did not excuse the petitioner from approaching the Area Level Committee, which he never did even after the modification order, leaving the original assessment order unchallenged before any competent authority.
cases.paras: the jurisdiction discussion (unnumbered order, orders dated 12.10.2011 and 18-19.10.2011)

UP-2005::2(oo).topic: 'Occupier' requires authorised occupation — tenant under an unstayed eviction decree

cases.title: Dr. Ashok Kumar Sharma & Another v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: 'Occupier' requires authorised occupation — tenant under an unstayed eviction decree
cases.holding: A tenant is ordinarily an 'occupier' (Clause 2(oo)) entitled to apply for a connection on an indemnity bond and cannot be denied supply merely for want of the landlord's NOC. But 'occupier' means a person authorised to occupy; a tenant faced with an unstayed eviction decree is not so authorised, and the court declined, in its discretion under Article 226, to direct a connection at that stage — with liberty to apply if the decree is set aside, recalled or stayed.

UP-2005::2.2.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.62(6)) with U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 2.2 definitions of tariff order/schedule, energy/demand/fixed charge)
UP-2005::2.2.clause: s.62(6) (interest only for overcharging above tariff) vis-a-vis a rebate under the tariff order
UP-2005::2.2.topic: Delayed crediting of a tariff-order rebate does not attract Section 62(6) interest, since a rebate is a bill-level concession, not itself part of the chargeable tariff

cases.title: M/S. Kamla Cold Storage And Ice Factory v. M.V.V.N.L. & Anr.
cases.topic: Delayed crediting of a tariff-order rebate does not attract Section 62(6) interest, since a rebate is a bill-level concession, not itself part of the chargeable tariff
cases.holding: No. Under Clause 2.2 of the Code, 'tariff order' and 'tariff schedule' fix the rates (fixed charge, energy charge, demand charge) a licensee may charge; a rebate is a distinct concession applied to reduce the bill generated from those tariff-calculated charges, not itself an element of the chargeable tariff. Since the fixed and energy charges billed to the consumer were correctly calculated as per the tariff order, and the rebate (also provided for in the tariff order) was in fact eventually credited, this is not a case of the licensee recovering a price or charge 'exceeding the tariff determined' within Section 62(6); a rebate cannot be equated to excessive tariff so as to bring delayed crediting within the ambit of Section 62(6). No interest was payable on the delayed rebate.

UP-2005::2.2(ss).topic: Recovery/sealing for a defaulter's dues is confined to the 'premises' for which the connection was sanctioned; scope disputes go to the Collector on facts

cases.title: M/S Birla Aircon v. District Magistrate, Meerut & Ors.
cases.topic: Recovery/sealing for a defaulter's dues is confined to the 'premises' for which the connection was sanctioned; scope disputes go to the Collector on facts
cases.holding: No, not without that determination. 'Premises' under Clause 2.2(ss) of the Code means the area/portion of the building/shed/field for which the connection was applied for or sanctioned to a single consumer; recovery as arrears of land revenue against the defaulter can proceed only against premises so defined. Since the record lacked sufficient material on the ownership/occupation of the two firms and the precise extent of the premises sanctioned to the defaulter (M/s Beeco Electricals India) as of the date of sanction (26.5.2004), the Court could not resolve the scope issue on the writ record and remitted the objection to the Collector (with liberty to conduct spot inspection) for a reasoned decision within three weeks, after hearing the licensee.

UP-2005::2.2(tt).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with UPERC Tariff Orders)
UP-2005::2.2(tt).topic: Protective-load charge requires the consumer's option and sanction

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.topic: Protective-load charge requires the consumer's option and sanction
cases.holding: No. A 'Protective Load' (Clause 2.2(tt): a load not subject to normal rostering) charge under the Tariff Orders is attracted only where the consumer has opted for the facility and it has been sanctioned by the licensee. The Aviation College never exercised such option; the demand — raised suo motu for eight years' arrears on an audit objection — was illegal (following Allahabad Inter Prises v. State of U.P.).

UP-2005::3.4.clause: 3.4(d)(ii) (consent of the 'original consumer' for tapping an independent feeder)
UP-2005::3.4.topic: Only the consumer who funded construction of the independent feeder itself is the 'original consumer' whose consent is needed for further tapping; a mere connecting-line-cost-bearing tapping consumer is not

cases.title: M/S Shri Parasnath Alloys (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Only the consumer who funded construction of the independent feeder itself is the 'original consumer' whose consent is needed for further tapping; a mere connecting-line-cost-bearing tapping consumer is not
cases.holding: No. The 'original consumer' whose consent is required under Clause 3.4(d)(ii) is the consumer at whose instance and cost the independent feeder itself was constructed — here, the consumer that paid the entire feeder-construction cost (over Rs. 1.25 crore) and was sanctioned load first. Subsequent consumers permitted to tap the feeder, who bore only the cost of their own connecting line (not the feeder's construction), do not thereby acquire 'original consumer' status or a consent right over further tapping; nor is there evidence that the petitioner itself obtained the true original consumer's consent, which would be necessary to stand in its shoes (as in Kesarwani Sheetalaya, factually distinguishable since there the objecting party had obtained consent from, and shared cost with, the true original consumer). Since the true original consumer raised no objection to the further sanction, and was not even a party to the writ, the petitioner (itself only a downstream tapping consumer) had no justiciable ground to object to a further consumer's tapping of the same feeder.

cases.title: Pawan Kumar Agarwal s/o M.P. Agarwal v. State of U.P. thru. Secretary & Ors.
cases.topic: Clause 3.4(a)'s list of industries requiring mandatory independent-feeder supply is specific/restrictive, not illustrative; consumers outside that list (or below the 1000 KVA threshold) have only an option, not an obligation, to take an independent feeder, and cannot be compelled to bear its cost where a shared feeder is technically feasible
cases.holding: No — Clause 3.4(a)'s enumerated industries (Arc/Induction furnaces, Rolling Mills, Re-rolling Mills, Mini steel plants) are specific and restrictive, not illustrative; a textile unit does not fall within it. Clause 3.4(b) gives such other consumers with load above 500 KVA merely an *option* to seek an independent feeder — it is not compulsory, and the licensee cannot insist on or compel independent-feeder supply where a dependent/shared feeder has been found technically feasible (as the respondents' own committee had found here). A generalized theft-prevention rationale does not override the Code's clear text, since the Code itself provides other anti-theft mechanisms. The condition imposed (independent-feeder connection, at ~Rs. 19 lakh cost to the consumer) was quashed, and the licensee directed to provide the sanctioned 3000 KVA connection from the existing 33 KV Fatehpur feeder within two weeks.

UP-2005::3.8.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.24(7), U.P. Electricity Reforms Act, 1999; Regulation 139, UPERC (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2004)
UP-2005::3.8.clause: 3.8(a) (tariff takes effect seven days after publication; no retrospective application)
UP-2005::3.8.topic: A revised tariff cannot be applied retrospectively to a date preceding its publication

cases.title: M/S Shokumbhari Pulp & Paper Mills Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & 3 Others (with connected petitions)
cases.topic: A revised tariff cannot be applied retrospectively to a date preceding its publication
cases.holding: No. Clause 3.8(a) of the Supply Code, read with Section 24(7) of the Reforms Act, 1999 and Regulation 139(2) of the 2004 Conduct of Business Regulations, provides that a published tariff takes effect only seven days after the last date of its publication in at least two widely-circulating daily newspapers, and remains in force until amended and published afresh; none of these provisions empowers retrospective application. Following Binani Zinc Ltd. v. Kerala SEB (the Regulatory Commission has not been empowered to frame tariff with retrospective effect, and all laws are presumptively prospective absent express provision or necessary intendment to the contrary), the licensee's notification purporting to apply the revised tariff from 1.10.2012 — though published only on 23.10.2012 and notified on 25.10.2012 — was without legal authority. The tariff was held effective only from 1.11.2012, and amounts realised on the earlier (retrospective) basis were directed to be adjusted in the consumers' future bills.

UP-2005::4.1.topic: Arrears-bar is premises-specific; connection to a tenant/occupier of a distinct premises

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Arrears-bar is premises-specific; connection to a tenant/occupier of a distinct premises
cases.holding: No. The arrears-bar in the third proviso to Clause 4.1 applies only to dues on the same 'premises' (Clause 2(ss)); the shop is a distinct premises and the tenant is an 'occupier' (Clause 2(oo)) entitled to apply. Clause 4.3(h) forbids refusal on the ground of dues on other portions; the licensee must instead pursue the defaulters under Clause 4.3(f)(v).

cases.title: Chandra Prakash Gupta v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Auction-purchaser and arrears — the Code as the missing statutory provision
cases.holding: No. Ahmedabad Electricity Co. v. Gujarat Inns turned on the absence of a statutory provision; Clause 4.1 of the 2005 Code (promulgated after that 2004 decision) now supplies one, requiring a No-Dues Certificate before a fresh connection on premises where ownership has changed and arrears exist. A SARFAESI auction-purchaser is bound by it and may obtain a connection only on furnishing a No-Dues Certificate.

UP-2005::4.20.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.47(5), EA 2003)
UP-2005::4.20.topic: Prepayment-meter exemption from security deposit is conditional on availability of the meter; Clause 4.20(l) not ultra vires s.47(5)

cases.title: M/S Dev Prayag Paper Mill (Pvt.) & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors. (batch of ~90 connected writ petitions)
cases.topic: Prepayment-meter exemption from security deposit is conditional on availability of the meter; Clause 4.20(l) not ultra vires s.47(5)
cases.holding: No, the clause is intra vires, and no, mere willingness does not suffice. Section 47(5) exempts a consumer from security only where the consumer is 'prepared' to take supply through a prepayment meter, and this preparedness is itself contingent on the actual availability of such a meter; Section 55 separately mandates only a 'correct meter', not a prepayment meter. Since prepayment meters for HT consumption are neither manufactured nor available in the Indian market, the licensee is under no obligation to install one merely on request, and the exemption in Section 47(5) does not arise. Clause 4.20(l) of the Supply Code, which links the exemption to the licensee 'providing a choice to consumer to opt' for a prepaid meter, does no more than track Section 47(5) and is not an independent or additional fetter; it is not ultra vires. Consequently, a demand for additional security on account of increased HT consumption, made while prepayment meters remain unavailable, is valid.

UP-2005::4.21(a).topic: System-loading charges — refundability where the connection is cancelled and never energised

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.topic: System-loading charges — refundability where the connection is cancelled and never energised
cases.holding: Yes, refundable. A system-loading charge is a compulsory exaction on one who enjoys the benefit of the distribution system; the liability accrues only once the applicant starts consuming electricity using the licensee's system. A prospective consumer who never takes supply cannot be fastened with it. Refund of Rs. 32,00,000 with interest @ 8.5% p.a. from the date of deposit ordered.

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Parallel-operating charges under pre-existing ("old") agreements
cases.holding: No. The clause preserves the charge only till termination and is read subject to the maxim that no party may take advantage of its own wrong. Charges end with actual disconnection (28.9.2007); the demand for January 2008-30.11.2018, with interest, is quashed.

UP-2005::4.3.topic: Clause 4.3(ii)-(iii) supports withholding a fresh connection pending dues, but does not by itself authorise coercive recovery of the previous owner's dues from a purchaser who never held the connection

cases.title: M/S Rayana Paper Board Industries Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Clause 4.3(ii)-(iii) supports withholding a fresh connection pending dues, but does not by itself authorise coercive recovery of the previous owner's dues from a purchaser who never held the connection
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.3(ii) obliges the vendor to clear outstanding dues before sale (or disclose them in the sale deed), and Clause 4.3(iii) allows the purchaser to seek a no-dues certificate, with the licensee bound to disclose pending dues or issue the certificate within 30 working days; the Code does not, however, contain any penal/recovery provision empowering the licensee to coercively recover the vendor's dues from the vendee. In the absence of a provision enabling such recovery, the licensee's right is confined to withdrawing/declining the electricity connection to the premises (i.e. refusing a fresh connection until dues are cleared, consistent with Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Paramount Polymers Pvt. Ltd.) — it cannot issue a coercive recovery citation against the purchaser for dues never incurred by the purchaser. The impugned recovery citation was quashed, with liberty to recover from the original owner (who, moreover, already had a pending dispute before the Electricity Ombudsman over the same dues).
cases.flag: An early (2010) ruling in the arrears/transferee cluster (cf. SCJ-005/012/031/036/037/054), drawing a distinction between (a) withholding a NEW connection pending dues (permissible leverage) and (b) coercive RECOVERY of the previous owner's dues from a non-consumer transferee (requires an express enabling provision). This narrower point about the mode of enforcement may retain force even after K.C. Ninan (SCJ-037) recognised that a Supply Code condition CAN create a statutory charge enabling recovery from a transferee where the Code so expressly provides.

UP-2005::4.3(f).topic: Liability of an auction-purchaser for arrears attaching to the premises

cases.title: Amir Ahmad v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Liability of an auction-purchaser for arrears attaching to the premises
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 4.3(f)(i) & (viii) place the duty to ascertain and clear outstanding dues on both seller and purchaser and permit the application to be processed only on clearance. The auction-purchaser, buying 'as-is-where-is', is fixed with 'buyer beware' and cannot escape the statutory charge by relying on the encumbrance-free recital or the vendor's non-consumption.

cases.title: Jitendra Kumar Gupta & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Subsequent purchaser liable for premises dues, including a theft assessment
cases.holding: Yes. 'Outstanding dues' under Clause 4.3(f) means all dues pending on the premises, including a post-theft assessment, and attach to the premises; the purchaser must obtain a No-Dues Certificate. The theft being a personal criminal liability of the previous occupant does not exclude the assessed civil amount. But recovery from the purchaser is subject to adjustment against any amount recovered from the original defaulter (no double recovery); here, a practical direction to deposit 50% to obtain the connection.

UP-2005::4.3(f)(v).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clauses 4.3(f)(v), 6.15) read with Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (ss.14, 31, 238) and Indian Contract Act, 1872 (s.128)
UP-2005::4.3(f)(v).clause: 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 (Director's liability for company's electricity dues) vis-a-vis IBC moratorium/resolution-plan discharge
UP-2005::4.3(f)(v).topic: Approval of a CIRP resolution plan and liquidation of the defaulter consumer-company does not extinguish a Director's independent personal-guarantor liability for the company's electricity dues; recovery against the Director under Clause 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 survives

cases.title: Narendra Singh Panwar v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Approval of a CIRP resolution plan and liquidation of the defaulter consumer-company does not extinguish a Director's independent personal-guarantor liability for the company's electricity dues; recovery against the Director under Clause 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 survives
cases.holding: No. The s.14 IBC moratorium, on its plain text, applies only to the Corporate Debtor and its own assets/proceedings — it has no application to a personal guarantor (State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan). Approval of a resolution plan under s.31 IBC does not ipso facto discharge a personal guarantor's independent, co-extensive liability under s.128 of the Contract Act (Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India); the release of the principal debtor by an involuntary process such as insolvency/liquidation does not absolve the guarantor. Since one of the Company's Directors had furnished a notarized undertaking/affidavit with the application for supply, undertaking to be liable for the Company's dues, and Clauses 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 of the Supply Code empower recovery against Directors as arrears of land revenue under the 1958 Dues Recovery Act, the demand notice against the Directors jointly was not vitiated merely by the Corporate Debtor's insolvency/liquidation. The vires challenge to Clause 4.3(f)(v) was not entertained for want of foundation in the pleadings. Writ petition dismissed.

UP-2005::4.3(g).topic: Pro-rata apportionment of arrears on a sub-divided premises

cases.title: Anubhav Jaiswal v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Pro-rata apportionment of arrears on a sub-divided premises
cases.holding: Only his pro-rata share. Though outstanding dues are the first charge on the premises (Clause 4.3(f)(iv)), on a legal sub-division they are apportioned pro-rata (Clause 4.3(g)) and a connection to the sub-divided portion is given on payment of that portion's share alone (Clause 4.3(h)); the licensee cannot demand the whole. The matter is remanded for fresh pro-rata determination after notice to the original owner.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. v. M/s DVS Steels & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Electricity dues are not a charge on the premises and cannot be recovered from a transferee absent contract/stipulation, but a distributor may lawfully condition a fresh connection to a sub-divided plot on pro-rata clearance of the predecessor's arrears
cases.holding: (a) No — electricity dues do not constitute a charge on the premises; a transferee with no privity of contract cannot be sued or subjected to revenue recovery for a predecessor's dues, absent a contract to the contrary. (b) Yes — this legal position affords no practical protection to a purchaser seeking a fresh connection: the distributor may validly stipulate, as a condition for supply, that a predecessor's arrears (or, for a legally sub-divided property, the pro-rata share under Clause 4.3(g)/(h)) be cleared first; such a condition is not unreasonable or arbitrary and legitimately protects the distributor against consumers evading dues by selling and relocating. (c) No — the purchaser here voluntarily paid the pro-rata dues as a condition for connection before any Commission order or injunction; a subsequent Commission direction restraining the distributor from *demanding* such payments from future applicants (issued because the predecessor furnished a bank guarantee for its disputed liability) did not itself direct refund of amounts already paid, and the purchaser — having paid pursuant to its own undertaking to obtain connection — is estopped from reclaiming it except on the agreed terms (i.e., refundable only if the predecessor's liability is ultimately negated or the predecessor actually clears the dues).

UP-2005::4.37.topic: Minimum-guarantee charges on temporary disconnection — only for consumer's default

cases.title: Harihar Cold Storage v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Minimum-guarantee charges on temporary disconnection — only for consumer's default
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.37 permits minimum-charge billing on a temporary disconnection only where the disconnection is on account of the consumer's default; here the disconnection was due to a burnt transformer the licensee failed to repair for about five months (breaching Clause 7.07's 24-hour restoration / 15-day replacement norms), so no minimum-guarantee charges lie. Where no fixed minimum sum is committed, minimum-guarantee charges require the licensee to ensure the minimum guaranteed supply.

UP-2005::4.4.topic: Tenant's connection on an indemnity bond absent owner's consent

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Tenant's connection on an indemnity bond absent owner's consent
cases.holding: Following Seema Mansoor, an occupier (including a tenant) has a statutory right to supply under Sections 42-43 read with Clause 4.4; where the owner's consent is unavailable, the tenant may file an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2) to obtain the connection.

cases.title: Devendra Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Clause 4.4 governs new connections, not disconnection over a landlord-tenant dispute
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.4 applies to new-connection applications, not to disconnecting an existing connection. A landlord-tenant dispute is not a ground to cut a valid connection on which bills are paid; a connection may be disconnected only on grounds authorised by the Act/Code (theft, unauthorised use, non-payment). The disconnection here was illegal, arbitrary and malafide, and offended Article 21.

cases.title: Divya Sahani v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.topic: Pendency of a property dispute is not a ground to refuse/disconnect a connection
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.4 does not prohibit a connection because of a pending property dispute; Clause 4.4(a)(i) only requires that a court-order copy be furnished where ownership is in litigation. A connection is not proof of title (Note-3, Annexure 4.1). Disconnection solely for the pendency of a suit is dehors the law and violates Article 21; mandamus issued to grant the connection.

cases.title: Gaurav Sharma v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Connection to a genuine occupier on an indemnity bond, without the owner's NOC
cases.holding: No. Section 43(1) confers on an occupier a statutory right to supply; Clause 4.4 read with Annexure 4.2 lets a genuine occupier unable to obtain the owner's NOC furnish an indemnity bond and obtain a connection. The object of the bond is only to exclude a trespasser/house-grabber; a family dispute or want of the owner's consent is no ground to refuse. Refusal quashed and remitted for reconsideration.

cases.title: Husna Bano v. State of U.P. & 9 Others
cases.topic: Tenant/occupier's connection on an indemnity bond amid a landlord-tenant dispute
cases.holding: No. Annexure 4.2 (Clause 4.4) enables an occupier who cannot obtain the owner's NOC to obtain a connection on an indemnity bond; possession can be shown by a Ration Card and Aadhaar (cash rent often leaving no receipt). The bond is not a document of title, and a connection does not bar an eviction suit; the landlord's refusal of NOC is no ground to deny supply. Refusal set aside and remitted for reconsideration.

cases.title: Mohd. Ashfaq Khan @ Ashfaq Khan v. State of U.P. thru. Addl. Chief Secy., Energy Deptt., Lucknow & 3 Others
cases.topic: An occupant/tenant whose connection was disconnected at the instance of a transferee-owner may seek a fresh connection under Clause 4.4 by furnishing an indemnity bond and proof of possession, subject to licensee inspection and without prejudice to the parties' civil rights
cases.holding: The petitioner was directed to apply for an electricity connection with an indemnity bond and proof of possession under Clause 4.4; the licensee may inspect to verify possession (hearing the transferee-owner in the process), and if there is no legal impediment and possession is proved, the connection shall be granted — without prejudice to either party's rights to pursue separate proceedings regarding possession/title.

cases.title: Priya Prem v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. & 4 Others
cases.topic: A new-connection grievance (including a s.43(3) penalty claim) is routed through the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum rather than decided directly in writ jurisdiction
cases.holding: The petitioner was directed to file a representation before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (presided over by the Sub Divisional Officer, Electricity Urban Distribution, Sub Division-IX Raptinagar, Gorakhpur) within two weeks; the Forum was directed to decide the representation within four weeks of receipt, by a reasoned order after affording the petitioner a hearing.

cases.title: Seema Mansoor v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & 3 Others
cases.topic: A tenant/occupier cannot be refused a new electricity connection solely for want of the landlord's consent, since the Supply Code provides an alternative indemnity-bond route (Annexure 4.2) precisely for such situations; refusing connection on landlord-consent grounds alone nullifies Rent Control Act protections and is against public policy
cases.holding: No. Section 43 of the Electricity Act, 2003 obliges the licensee to supply electricity to any owner OR occupier (a term the Supply Code, Clause 2.2(oo), defines to include an authorised person in occupation, i.e. a tenant) making a proper application. While Clause 4.4(a)(i) of the Code lists owner's consent (Annexure 4.3) among required documents, the Code simultaneously provides Annexure 4.2 — an indemnity bond specifically designed for the situation where 'the intending consumer is not the owner' and 'is not able to obtain the consent' of the owner — as an alternative route, indemnifying the licensee against loss/claims from the owner, recoverable under the Revenue Recovery Act if needed. Reading the Code holistically, a tenant cannot be denied connection merely for lack of landlord consent; to hold otherwise would let an unscrupulous landlord (here, one in an ongoing rent dispute who had already gotten the existing connection disconnected to pressure the tenant to vacate) defeat Rent Control Act protections by simply withholding consent — an interpretation contrary to both the statutory scheme and public policy. Two prior Division Bench rulings to the contrary (Ravi Shankar Giri; the Iftikhar Ahsan/Tanveer Azam line) were held not to lay down correct law, having overlooked ss.42/43 of the Act and Clause 4.4(a)(i)/Annexure 4.2 of the Code. Mandamus issued directing the licensee to consider and grant connection to the petitioner-tenant, subject to a proper application, indemnity bond, and fulfilment of other requirements.

UP-2005::4.49.topic: Load reduction with disputed arrears — Bond acceptable; effective date; agreed reduction cannot be defeated

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. M/s L.M.L. Limited & Ors.
cases.topic: Load reduction with disputed arrears — Bond acceptable; effective date; agreed reduction cannot be defeated
cases.holding: No. The unamended Clause 4.49 (in force on 19.4.2006) allowed the consumer to secure disputed arrears by a Bank Guarantee OR a Bond OR any instrument to the licensee's satisfaction; the reduction took effect from the first day of the month after sanction (Clause 4.41(e), i.e. 1.5.2006). Having agreed to the reduction and known of the consumer's Relief-Undertaking/Sick-Company status and the BIFR order, the licensee acted unfairly in rejecting the Bond, insisting on a Bank Guarantee and continuing to bill on the higher (8 MVA) load; the load stood reduced.

UP-2005::4.5(d).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 4.5(d)) read with the Works of Licensees Rules, 2006 (Clause 3)
UP-2005::4.5(d).clause: 4.5(d) (landowner's right to object to a supply line over his land) read with Works of Licensees Rules, 2006, Clause 3 (resolution mechanism)
UP-2005::4.5(d).topic: A landowner's objection to an electric pole/line erected on his private property to supply neighbouring residents is to be resolved by the District Magistrate/Commissioner of Police/authorised officer under Clause 3 of the Works of Licensees Rules, 2006, balancing his Clause 4.5(d) right against the public interest in the electrification work

cases.title: Priy Shankar Pandey v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: A landowner's objection to an electric pole/line erected on his private property to supply neighbouring residents is to be resolved by the District Magistrate/Commissioner of Police/authorised officer under Clause 3 of the Works of Licensees Rules, 2006, balancing his Clause 4.5(d) right against the public interest in the electrification work
cases.holding: The landowner has a right under Clause 4.5(d) of the Supply Code to object to a supply line being laid over his land; that objection is to be resolved under Clause 3 of the Works of Licensees Rules, 2006 by the District Magistrate, Commissioner of Police, or other authorised officer, who must balance the landowner's rights against the public interest in not unduly stalling the electrification work. The petitioner was directed to file an application under Clause 3 (with a supporting affidavit, documents, and photographs) within three weeks; the authority was directed to decide the application within eight weeks after hearing all necessary parties, with status quo to be maintained in the interim.

cases.title: Shivmahraj v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.topic: Companion ruling to SCJ-104 — identical holding on a parallel landowner objection to a new power line/pole for village electrification
cases.holding: As in SCJ-104: the landowner has a right under Clause 4.5(d) of the Supply Code to object to a supply line/pole being erected over his land; that objection is to be resolved under Clause 3 of the Works of Licensees Rules, 2006 by the District Magistrate or other authorised officer, balancing the landowner's rights against the public interest in the electrification work. The petitioner was directed to appear before the District Magistrate (already scheduled to hear similar grievances) with all relevant material, to be heard and a decision passed after hearing all parties including the licensee respondents, with status quo maintained in the interim.
cases.flag: Near-identical companion order to SCJ-104; recorded compactly given the substantially duplicate reasoning and holding.

UP-2005::5.6.topic: Check-meter procedure under Clause 5.6 is triggered only by the consumer's request; silence on the meter's slow-running finding forfeits the objection

cases.title: M/S Krown Bakers India Pvt. Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam & Anr.
cases.topic: Check-meter procedure under Clause 5.6 is triggered only by the consumer's request; silence on the meter's slow-running finding forfeits the objection
cases.holding: No. Clause 5.6 gives the licensee the right to test a meter on reasonable doubt of accuracy, and separately gives the consumer the right to request testing (including installation of a check meter) if he doubts the meter's accuracy; the obligation to install a check meter arises only on the consumer's request. Since the consumer had full knowledge from the sealing certificate that the meter was found running slow, never disputed that finding or sought a check-meter test — his representations and applications (including a request for installment payment) challenged only the bill, not the meter's operational status — he cannot now contend that the bill is vitiated for non-compliance with Clause 5.6.

cases.title: M/S Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
cases.topic: Clause 5.6 applies to testing of 'any meter', not only a known-defective one; meter-manufacturer's own lab is not an 'independent laboratory'; procedural safeguards must be followed
cases.holding: (a) No, the heading does not confine the clause: a marginal heading/side-note is not a legitimate aid to statutory construction (Chandler v. DPP; Chandroji Rao v. CIT; Padmaraje R. Kadambande v. CIT; Guntaiah v. Hambamma; followed in Ghanshyam Gupta v. United India Insurance). Clause 5.6(a) gives the licensee the right to test 'any meter' on reasonable doubt of accuracy, which includes a meter that has stopped recording despite continued consumption. (b) No — testing by the meter's own manufacturer is not testing by an 'independent laboratory'; a commercial manufacturer with a business interest in its product's reputation for being tamper/pilfer-proof cannot be an unbiased arbiter, offending the principle that no one may be a judge in his own cause (following the Patna High Court's JMD Alloys Ltd. v. Bihar SEB, which deprecated testing of Secure Meters by their own manufacturer as creating a strong bias). Further, the Clause 5.6(d) safeguards (advance notice of the testing date, opportunity for the consumer/representative to be present, signature on the test result sheet) were not followed before the manufacturer's report was obtained, and this defect was never addressed by either the Assessing Officer or the Appellate Authority.

cases.title: M/S Santosh Preservation Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr.
cases.topic: Independent-laboratory testing right under Clause 5.6(c)(iii) applies only where the tampering/defect conclusion rests on a test report, not where tampering is patent on inspection
cases.holding: No. Clause 5.6(c)(iii)'s independent-testing option exists to rule out bias where the conclusion of a fast/slow-running or tampered meter is arrived at on the basis of a test report (i.e. where the defect is not visible on inspection and needs laboratory ascertainment) — as in Mohd. Sagir and Smt. Amrawati Devi, both distinguished here. Where, as here, tampering is obvious to the naked eye at inspection itself (window/TP seals tampered, R and B phase wires cut, the meter recording nil consumption though the transformer showed live current on all three phases), the conclusion of theft does not depend on any test report; the licensee's subsequent sending of the meter for testing (for record purposes) does not confer a Clause 5.6(c)(iii) right that never arose. Since the tampering was a foregone conclusion on the inspection report itself, the assessment order was not vitiated for want of independent testing or for being non-speaking, and interference under Article 226 was declined.

cases.title: M/S Venus Stone Crushing Co. & Anr. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Mandatory pre-testing notice (now final per SC's SLP dismissal in Amrawati Devi); licensee bears the burden of proving the consumer, not an intervening cause, caused the irregularity; manufacturer's lab is not independent
cases.holding: No. Paras 5.17/5.18/5.20 of the 2002 Code (materially identical to Clause 5.6 of the 2005 Code) mandate seven days' advance notice of any laboratory testing so the consumer may be present; this is a mandatory procedure per Amrawati Devi v. PVVNL, a ruling since rendered final by the Supreme Court's dismissal of the SLP against it (3.8.2009) — a test report obtained without this procedure cannot ground any action against the consumer. Since the sealing certificate at removal recorded only a burnt meter (no tampered/defective seals) and unrelated CT/PT phase errors that were also technically explicable and had self-corrected without any external intervention, the subsequent 'tampering' finding of the manufacturer's own lab (obtained ex parte, undated, and after the meter had left the consumer's custody) could not be relied upon; the licensee bears the burden of proving with cogent evidence that the consumer, rather than some cause arising after the meter's removal, caused the alleged irregularity. Following Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL and JMD Alloys v. Bihar SEB, a meter manufacturer's own laboratory is not an 'independent laboratory'. Since the assessment's very basis (the test report) was vitiated, and the Clause 6.8/Ashok Kumar assessment procedure was also not followed, the entire assessment fell.

UP-2005::5.6(d).topic: Meter-testing procedure vs a compounded theft offence

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Meter-testing procedure vs a compounded theft offence
cases.holding: No. Once the sum is paid under Section 152(1) and the offence is deemed compounded, the tampering stands admitted-compounded and the question of following the meter-testing procedure (para 5.6(d)) does not arise. The theft assessment was made on the Code's formula (Annexure 6.3); the procedural challenge fails.

cases.title: Saurabh Agrawal & Another v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Continued s.135 theft prosecution is quashed as an abuse of process where the underlying consumer inspection report does not itself allege theft, the licensee's own subsequent conduct treated the matter as slow metering (fully paid under Clause 5.6(c)(ii)), the Clause 5.6(d) meter-testing procedure (including MRI/proper laboratory testing) was not followed, and the s.127 appellate authority already conclusively held (with finality) that s.135 was inapplicable on the same facts
cases.holding: Yes — quashed. The consumer inspection report dated 2.8.2007, the sole evidentiary basis for the FIR/charge-sheet, did not itself record an allegation of theft (the relevant column was struck through); the licensee's parallel conduct — assessing and fully recovering the disputed amount (Rs. 71,95,449) as slow-metering charges under Clause 5.6(c)(ii) — was inconsistent with treating the same facts as theft. The Clause 5.6(d) procedure (notice of testing date, opportunity to be present, right to dispute per 5.6(c)) was never followed; no MRI report was obtained, and the seized meter was left at the police station rather than sent for proper laboratory testing, undermining any theft finding. The appellate authority under s.127 (Additional Commissioner, Judicial-II, Saharanpur) had, in a final order dated 24.10.2008 (upheld by a separate writ petition and never further challenged), held that s.135 was inapplicable and directed revision of the bills — a finding of finality directly negating the criminal prosecution's premise. Continuing the s.135 prosecution on the same consumer inspection report, after these developments, amounts to an abuse of the process of law within the settled Prakash P. Hinduja standard, and the charge-sheet, cognizance order, and pending proceedings were accordingly quashed.

UP-2005::6.1(g).topic: Billing/disconnection window — 15-day bill dispatch plus disconnection notice

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Billing/disconnection window — 15-day bill dispatch plus disconnection notice
cases.holding: No. Clause 6.1(g) requires the bill to be dispatched at least 15 days before the due date, and a further seven days' notice is contemplated before disconnection; here the bill (issued 28.03.2011, due 31.03.2011) gave only three days and the disconnection (08.04.2011) preceded the statutory window, rendering it illegal. Ante-dating the payment receipt to 31.03.2011 was also illegal manipulation of the record.

UP-2005::6.14.topic: Consumer may seek payment of outstanding dues in installments under Clause 6.14

cases.title: Kripa Shanker v. State of U.P. Thru. Distt. Collector, Unnao & Ors.
cases.topic: Consumer may seek payment of outstanding dues in installments under Clause 6.14
cases.holding: Clause 6.14 of the Code already provides for payment of outstanding dues in installments; on an application by the consumer, the Executive Engineer must consider and decide the request expeditiously. By consent, the Court directed the petitioner to deposit Rs. 15,000 and move a Clause 6.14 application, staying recovery pending decision, conditional on the deposit being made.

UP-2005::6.15.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clauses 6.15, 4.36, 4.38) read with Electricity Act, 2003 (s.56(2))
UP-2005::6.15.clause: 6.15(1)(b) (2-year recovery bar) read with 4.36 (mandatory temporary-disconnection duty) and 4.38(c) (permanent disconnection requiring consumer affidavit)
UP-2005::6.15.topic: The Clause 6.15/s.56(2) two-year recovery bar imposes a positive obligation on the licensee to act (notice, then temporary disconnection under Clause 4.36) within that window; prolonged licensee silence (here, ~12 years with no demand notice) forfeits the right to recover, and Clause 4.38(c)'s affidavit requirement for permanent disconnection cannot be invoked in isolation to defeat this bar

cases.title: Satya Narayan v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. thru. its Managing Director & Others
cases.topic: The Clause 6.15/s.56(2) two-year recovery bar imposes a positive obligation on the licensee to act (notice, then temporary disconnection under Clause 4.36) within that window; prolonged licensee silence (here, ~12 years with no demand notice) forfeits the right to recover, and Clause 4.38(c)'s affidavit requirement for permanent disconnection cannot be invoked in isolation to defeat this bar
cases.holding: No, not beyond the two-year window contemplated by Clause 6.15(1)(b)/s.56(2), absent evidence the sum was continuously shown as recoverable arrears. Reading the Supply Code as a whole (not piecemeal), Clause 4.36 casts a mandatory obligation on the licensee to issue notice and proceed with temporary disconnection upon non-payment within the statutory window; a licensee's total silence for ~12 years, without a single demand notice, forecloses reliance on Clause 4.38(c) (permanent disconnection contingent on the consumer's own affidavit clearing dues) to justify a stale recovery — that clause operates subject to, not independent of, the licensee's own Clause 4.36/6.15 obligations. The Court moulded relief: the petitioner was permitted to seek refund of any amount paid in excess of what would be recoverable for a proper two-year period, and the Corporation was directed to issue a circular/order sensitising its employees to their Supply Code duties, given the demonstrated departmental negligence.

UP-2005::6.16.topic: Protective treatment of sick industrial companies / relief undertakings

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. M/s L.M.L. Limited & Ors.
cases.topic: Protective treatment of sick industrial companies / relief undertakings
cases.holding: Clauses 4.41 and 4.49 are Rules framed to help industries in difficulty; read with Annexure 6.5 / Clause 6.16 (disconnected units seeking revival) and Clause 9.5 (Relief Undertaking regime under s.23), only current dues are realized from a sick/relief undertaking, with past dues recovered in instalments and no coercive disconnection — harmonised with the BIFR/SICA order.

UP-2005::6.5.topic: Billing disputes — alternative remedy of complaint before the Competent Authority

cases.title: Chandrika v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Billing disputes — alternative remedy of complaint before the Competent Authority
cases.holding: A dispute as to the correctness of a bill is to be raised by complaint before the Competent Authority (the Executive Engineer) under Clause 6.5 of the Code; the writ petition is disposed of by relegating the consumer to that remedy, with a direction to decide by a speaking order after hearing and interim protection from coercive recovery conditioned on a part-deposit (Rs. 20,000).

cases.title: Lala Ram Batham v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam & Ors.
cases.topic: Disputed meter reading relegated to a Clause 6.5 representation, with mandatory inspection of the removed meter
cases.holding: Under Clause 6.5 of the Code, the consumer may raise the grievance by representation before the licensee, who must decide it expeditiously by a speaking order after hearing the consumer; before deciding, the licensee must personally inspect the removed (old) meter to verify the correctness of the disputed reading. The writ court did not adjudicate the claim on merits.

cases.title: Prem Singh v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Dispute over assessment of an electricity bill relegated to the Clause 6.5 authority
cases.holding: The petitioner is permitted to approach the Executive Engineer (Rural), Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd., Fatehgarh, District Farrukhabad by invoking Clause 6.5 of the Supply Code for redressal of the billing assessment dispute.

UP-2005::6.5(b).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clauses 5.5, 5.6, 5.6(c)(iii), 6.5(b)) read with s.162, Electricity Act, 2003
UP-2005::6.5(b).clause: 6.5(b) (Disputed Bills and Arrears) read with 5.6 (meter testing)
UP-2005::6.5(b).topic: A supplementary bill grounded in a disputed/defective meter or transformer reading is a 'disputed bill' under Clause 6.5(b); the consumer must first invoke the Clause 5.6 meter-testing procedure (and thereafter the Electrical Inspector) rather than approaching the writ court directly

cases.title: Mohamdabad Cold Storage Private Ltd. (& Anr.) v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: A supplementary bill grounded in a disputed/defective meter or transformer reading is a 'disputed bill' under Clause 6.5(b); the consumer must first invoke the Clause 5.6 meter-testing procedure (and thereafter the Electrical Inspector) rather than approaching the writ court directly
cases.holding: A supplementary bill founded on a disputed meter/transformer reading falls within Clause 6.5(b)'s 'disputed bills' notwithstanding its heading; since the bill cannot be assessed without first resolving the accuracy of the underlying meter/instrument reading, the consumer must invoke the Clause 5.6 (and 5.6(c)(iii)) meter-testing procedure, and if unresolved, approach the Electrical Inspector under s.162 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (the modern successor, per Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Undertaking v. Laffans (India) Pvt. Ltd., to the Electrical Inspector's statutory-arbitration role under the 1910 Act). The writ petition, filed without first exhausting this route, is premature and dismissed without costs, without prejudice to the petitioners' right to raise their grievance before the authority concerned or the Electrical Inspector.

cases.title: Mother India Refrigeration Industries (& Anr.) v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Companion ruling to SCJ-083 — identical holding on a parallel supplementary-bill dispute grounded in a defective transformer
cases.holding: As in SCJ-083: a supplementary bill founded on a disputed/defective transformer reading is a 'disputed bill' under Clause 6.5(b); the consumer must first invoke the Clause 5.6 meter-testing procedure and, if unresolved, the Electrical Inspector under s.162 of the Electricity Act, 2003, rather than approach the writ court directly. The writ petition is premature and dismissed without costs, without prejudice to the petitioners' right to raise their grievance before the authority concerned or the Electrical Inspector.
cases.flag: Near-verbatim companion order to SCJ-083; recorded compactly to avoid duplicating the identical reasoning.

UP-2005::6.5B.topic: Dispute over the quantum of a demand notice is relegated to the authority under Clause 6.5B

cases.title: Madarsa Dargah Aaliya Islamiya Shareef Nagar & Anr. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Dispute over the quantum of a demand notice is relegated to the authority under Clause 6.5B
cases.holding: The consumer is permitted to approach the authority concerned under Clause 6.5B of the Code, which must examine the objection raised as to quantification and pass a reasoned order within six weeks of presentation of a certified copy of the court's order.

UP-2005::6.8.topic: Reasonable opportunity of hearing before a theft-based final assessment; procedural defect condoned where opportunity was in substance given

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.topic: Reasonable opportunity of hearing before a theft-based final assessment; procedural defect condoned where opportunity was in substance given
cases.holding: Reasonable opportunity of hearing in a theft assessment is governed by Clauses 6.8(b)(i), 6.8(c)(iii) read with 8.1(b) of the Code (citing Khem Chand v. Union of India and Transmission Corporation of A.P. v. Sri Rama Krishna Rice Mill on the nature of 'reasonable opportunity'). Provisional assessment, reply, and final assessment together form a single process reaching finality; where the authority afforded an opportunity for hearing (including through consideration of a representation directed by an earlier writ order) before making the final assessment, any procedural defect at the provisional stage is condoned, since procedural law cannot override the substantive law.

cases.title: Latif v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Mandatory Clause 6.8 procedure for unauthorised-use assessment; bypassing it via the 1958 Recovery of Dues Act is illegal
cases.holding: No. Following Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P., Clause 6.8 requires: (a) a site inspection report disclosing the irregularity, handed to the consumer or pasted/posted if refused; (b) a show-cause notice with the provisional assessment, giving 15 working days for reply and fixing a hearing date; and (c) after personal hearing, a speaking final order within 7 working days recording whether unauthorised use is established and the assessed amount. Since no such show-cause notice was issued and no final order under Clause 6.8(c) was passed, a bill-cum-notice and demand notice issued instead under Section 5 of the 1958 Act is illegal and inconsistent with the prescribed procedure; it is set aside, without prejudice to the licensee proceeding afresh in accordance with the Clause 6.8/Ashok Kumar procedure.

cases.title: M/S Kissan Chilling Udyog & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: A theft assessment resting on a misreading of the checking report (conflating the main meter and a separately-installed double/test meter) cannot sustain
cases.holding: No. Following Ashok Kumar's Clause 6.8 procedure (inspection report, 15-working-day show-cause notice, hearing, speaking final order), the impugned orders were quashed for two independent defects: (1) no valid Clause 6.8 notice/final order was issued disclosing the manner of the alleged unauthorised use or the basis for the assessed quantum, and (2) the notice and final order misread the checking report by attributing tampering ('all seals found tempered') to the main meter and treating the double meter's contents as equally condemnatory, when the checking report showed the body-seal defect recorded only for the main meter and the foreign device only inside the double meter (installed by the respondents themselves to test the main meter, under no averred common sealing certificate) — a misreading respondent's own counsel conceded justified remand. The Assessing Authority was given liberty to reassess afresh strictly per Clause 6.8 and Ashok Kumar.

cases.title: M/S Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
cases.topic: A Section 126 assessment (being penal/fiscal-preventive) cannot include dues not contemplated by the statute (e.g. electricity duty), and minimum-charge liability during disconnection requires fault attributable to the consumer
cases.holding: Since a Section 126/Clause 6.8 assessment amount is expressly excluded from computation of the consumer's monthly/annual charge liability, the assessment being penal in scope cannot be enlarged to add other dues (here, electricity duty) not contemplated by the statute. Separately, minimum consumption/guarantee charges for a period of disconnection can be demanded only where the disconnection is attributable to the consumer's own fault (e.g. an established theft justifying disconnection); where the fault (or its absence) is unresolved, the licensee cannot claim such charges, and the billing authority must determine responsibility for the disconnection before raising the demand.

cases.title: M/S Sartaj Rice Mill Thru' Its Partner Maqsood Ali v. Paschimanchal Vidhyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: An assessment accepted by the consumer's own offer to pay in instalments becomes final/binding; opportunity of hearing was satisfied where the consumer was present but failed to substantiate his objection, and an adjournment could not override a court-mandated deadline
cases.holding: No. The consumer's own written offer (19.10.2001) to pay the assessed dues in instalments, accepted by the Executive Engineer with restoration of supply, rendered the earlier assessments final by his own conduct; a subsequent, undisputed third notice (based on actual meter inspection reports) stood in the same position. Para 3.1, Chapter 7 of the Commercial and Revenue Manual (read with Clause 6.8(c)(i) of the Code) required an opportunity of hearing before assessment/recovery, which was afforded pursuant to this Court's earlier order directing disposal of the consumer's 04.05.2005 objection within four weeks; the consumer was present at the hearing but failed to produce the documents (copy of his representation/receipt) he claimed supported his case, and his advocate's illness-based adjournment request on the last available date could not be granted without breaching the court's deadline. No ex parte order or breach of natural justice was made out.

cases.title: M/S Urmila Oil Industries v. U.P. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam & Ors.
cases.topic: An assessment based on mere 'possibility of theft' inferred from an MRI pattern, without Clause 6.8 procedure or reasoned analysis, cannot be sustained
cases.holding: No. The impugned notice itself stated only that the consumer's system 'has given rise to a possibility of direct theft of electricity' from the recorded nil night-time load; no specific reason was given for how the authorities concluded theft had occurred, nor was the manner of assessment disclosed, nor was the Clause 6.8 show-cause procedure followed. The consumer's explanation (that a transformer protection device disconnected supply at night as a safety measure during non-production hours) was rejected as 'unsatisfactory and illogical' without reasoned engagement. Following Ashok Kumar v. State of U.P., the assessment and demand were set aside for non-compliance with Section 126 read with Clause 6.8, with liberty to the Assessing Authority to pass a fresh order in accordance with law.

cases.title: Mohd Usman Ansari v. Chairman, Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. & 4 Others
cases.topic: A recovery certificate founded on an ex-parte provisional s.126 assessment, issued without following the Supply Code's assessment procedure, entitles the consumer to a hearing and a reasoned final assessment before coercive recovery
cases.holding: The Court directed that an opportunity of hearing be granted to the petitioner, with a final assessment to be carried out by the authorities within 12 weeks; until the final assessment order is passed, no coercive recovery measures may be taken against the petitioner.

cases.title: Mrs Rajendra Kumar Sharma v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: A s.126 final assessment order that does not address the consumer's objections, fix a hearing date, or record theft findings breaches Clauses 6.8/8.1; the recovery citation founded on it must be withdrawn and a fresh assessment made after due notice and hearing
cases.holding: No — the licensee's own two-member inquiry committee found that Clauses 6.8 and 8.1 of the Supply Code had not been followed by the assessing Executive Engineer; the recovery citation founded on the impugned final assessment was directed to be cancelled, a fresh notice with objections and a hearing was issued, disciplinary show-cause proceedings were initiated against the officer, and a fresh final assessment order was to be passed within ten days. Pending that fresh assessment, the Court directed restoration of electricity supply on the petitioner depositing Rs. 25,00,000/- as security, subject to the outcome of the fresh assessment.

cases.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: A final assessment order passed more than two years after the provisional assessment notice, without affording a fresh opportunity to object, violates natural justice and is liable to be set aside notwithstanding an available s.127 appellate remedy, where the assessing officer's jurisdiction itself is challenged
cases.holding: Section 126(3) contemplates a final assessment ordinarily within 30 days of the provisional assessment order; where, as here, more than two years elapsed between the provisional assessment notice (23.5.2011) and the final assessment order (21.6.2013) with no fresh notice or opportunity given, the final assessment order cannot be said to have been passed in consonance with natural justice, notwithstanding the petitioner's failure to object to the original provisional notice and the availability of an appeal under s.127. The recovery citation was set aside, and the petitioner was directed to file objections to the (revived) provisional assessment notice within 15 days, with the Executive Engineer to pass a fresh final assessment decision within one month, leaving the respondents free to proceed further in accordance with law thereafter.

cases.title: Sanjay Rizvi v. M.D. Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. & Others
cases.topic: A provisional assessment for alleged unauthorised use/theft, made without authentic verification data (e.g. MRI testing of the seized meter, despite the licensee's own procedure contemplating it and a specific court direction to obtain instructions on it), and without full compliance with the Clause 6.8 hearing procedure, is impugnable; the consumer is relegated to a fresh, properly-conducted departmental assessment process with preserved appeal rights, rather than a writ-court determination of the underlying factual dispute
cases.holding: The provisional assessment notice did not appear to have an authentic evidentiary basis; Clause 6.8 of the Supply Code requires that before concluding unauthorised use of electricity, the consumer be given an opportunity (inspection report communicated, show-cause notice with objections invited, personal hearing, then a speaking final order) — a requirement rooted in natural justice given the serious, offence-adjacent nature of the allegation. Given that an equally efficacious alternative remedy exists and the underlying factual/technical controversy (correctness of the alleged theft-detection method, given the absence of MRI verification) is better assessed by persons with technical expertise than by the writ court, the petition was disposed of by directing the petitioner to file a fresh representation (annexing the writ petition) before the licensee, to be decided by a reasoned, speaking order after a hearing addressing whether unauthorised use is established; if established, a final assessment order was to follow (for the full period per Clause 6.8(c)(iii)), appealable under s.127 read with Clause 6.8(d).

UP-2005::6.8(d).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (read with s.127, Electricity Act 2003)
UP-2005::6.8(d).topic: Remedy against a final theft assessment — statutory appeal under s.127 / Clause 6.8(d)

cases.title: Dr. Santosh Kumar Awasthi v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Remedy against a final theft assessment — statutory appeal under s.127 / Clause 6.8(d)
