cases.holding: The remedy against a final order of assessment is the statutory appeal under Section 127 read with Clause 6.8(d) of the Code, on deposit of half the assessed amount; the writ court relegated the consumer to that appeal, directing it be entertained without a limitation objection, staying recovery for 30 days, and leaving the merits and any stay to the appellate authority.

UP-2005::6.9.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.126, EA 2003 & Tariff Order)
UP-2005::6.9.topic: Excess load / appliance installation is not 'unauthorised use' under Section 126

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.topic: Excess load / appliance installation is not 'unauthorised use' under Section 126
cases.holding: It is not Section 126 unauthorised use. Para 6.9 of the Code provides that excess load is not covered by Section 126; the use of an air conditioner is not prohibited but attracts an additional Fixed Charge under the tariff (Rs. 150 per ton, April-September). The CGRF/Ombudsman rightly disallowed the Section 126 assessment and permitted only supplementary Fixed-Charge bills.

UP-2005::7.10.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.42(5)-(7), EA 2003; UPERC (CGRF & Ombudsman) Regulations)
UP-2005::7.10.topic: Only the consumer, not the Distribution Licensee, may approach the Forum or the Ombudsman

cases.title: M.K. Pathak, Executive Engineer v. The Electricity Ombudsman & Ors.
cases.topic: Only the consumer, not the Distribution Licensee, may approach the Forum or the Ombudsman
cases.holding: No. Clause 7.10 of the Code and Section 42(5)-(7) of the Act, on a plain reading, entitle only the consumer to file a complaint before the Forum and, if aggrieved by non-redressal, a representation before the Ombudsman; this right is not given to the Electricity Distribution Licensee. The licensee/its officers therefore have no authority in law to approach the Ombudsman once the Forum has decided the consumer's complaint, and the Ombudsman commits no error of law in dismissing such a representation, even on its merits.

cases.title: M/S Three Star Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 5 Ors.
cases.topic: A consumer who accepted a One Time Settlement covering 'all pending matters' is estopped from later reviving one of the settled disputes through the CGRF/Ombudsman route
cases.holding: No. The consumer's own representation accepting the One Time Settlement made clear it was 'ready to settle its ALL pending matters' by paying the agreed principal sum; the licensee accepted this and waived more than Rs. 78 lakh of accrued surcharge. Having obtained that benefit on the basis that all disputes stood settled, the consumer is estopped from raising the 10%-rebate dispute afresh before the Redressal Forum/Ombudsman; both correctly rejected the claim.

cases.title: Om Prakash v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: A billing grievance pending before the District Consumer Forum should instead be routed through the licensee's Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum and, if unresolved, the Ombudsman under Clause 7.10
cases.holding: The petitioner was permitted to withdraw his writ petition and his pending District Consumer Forum complaint in order to approach the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum under Clause 7.10 of the Supply Code; the concerned authority was directed to decide the grievance, if presented within 15 days, as expeditiously as possible and not later than 8 weeks from presentation of a certified copy of the order.

UP-2005::8.1.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.126, EA 2003 & 1958 Dues Recovery Act)
UP-2005::8.1.topic: Proper assessment (with hearing) is a precondition to recovery

cases.title: Gauri Shankar Gupta v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Proper assessment (with hearing) is a precondition to recovery
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(a)&(b) read with Section 126 require notice, service of the provisional assessment, and an opportunity of hearing before a final assessment; only on such an assessment, and non-payment of the demand thereunder, can recourse be had to the 1958 Act. The department failed to show the demand notice was served or that any assessment order was passed; the recovery order and citation are quashed, with liberty to reassess after hearing.

cases.title: M/S Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Anr. v. PVVNL & Ors.
cases.topic: Theft cannot be inferred from an unexplained divergence between the billing meter and untested outside check-meters
cases.holding: No. Under para 8.1(b)(iv) of the Code, a case of theft must be established, not presumed. Since the three outside meters (maintained under the licensee's own seal/custody) recorded consumption comparable to the billing meter for nearly the whole assessment period, were never independently tested, and no report of tampering with them was ever lodged, there was no material basis to infer theft at the consumer's premises merely from a late-period divergence (occurring only around the time the billing meter was destroyed by fire); an unsupported suggestion at the hearing that all four meters had been remotely tampered could not be explained by the licensee's own technical officer and did not constitute evidence. The assessment and confirming appellate order (itself unreasoned/non-speaking, contrary to para 8.1) were quashed.

cases.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
cases.topic: A 'final notice' demanding payment of a provisionally assessed amount, issued without any hearing on the consumer's timely-filed objections and without an actual reasoned final assessment order, is dehors the Section 126/Clause 8.1 procedure and must be quashed
cases.holding: No. Section 126(1)'s provisional assessment requires the assessing officer's recorded conclusion of unauthorised use, which itself cannot be reached without a fair opportunity of hearing given the potential overlap with s.135 investigation. Clause 8.1(b)(iii) of the Supply Code specifically requires a personal hearing after the consumer files objections to the provisional assessment/show-cause notice, before any final order is passed. Here, after the petitioner filed timely objections (pursuant to an earlier court order permitting him to do so and deposit 50% of the provisional amount for restoration), the licensee neither gave notice of hearing nor considered the objections, yet issued 'final notice' letters (4.3.2017, repeated 17.3.2017) simply reiterating the original provisional-assessment figure as though finally established, without ever serving any actual reasoned final assessment order. This is dehors the statutory procedure (following Ashok Kumar, Kamil, and Hazi Mohd. Yaseen) — a consumer cannot be compelled to pay a provisional-assessment amount as if final, absent a proper final assessment after hearing. The two impugned notices were quashed, with liberty to the licensee to conduct the final assessment properly, in accordance with the Act and the Code.

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: For assessment of theft of electricity under s.135, Clauses 8.1/8.2 of the Supply Code (not Clause 6.8) govern; Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires 15 working days' show-cause notice and Clause 8.1(b)(iv) mandates assessment at 1.5 times (not 3 times) the applicable tariff if theft is established after hearing
cases.holding: Following Mohit Paper Mills (applying the specific-prevails-over-general canon), Clauses 8.1/8.2 govern theft-based assessment, not Clause 6.8. On the facts, the assessing officer's provisional-assessment notice (25.5.2007) gave only one week (not the mandated 15 working days), lacked specificity as to which s.135(1) clause was invoked, and calculated the provisional assessment at thrice (not 1.5 times) the applicable tariff — all procedural lapses reflecting negligence or lack of legal clarity by the (technically-trained, non-legal) assessing officer, for which the licensee bears responsibility to provide adequate training. However, since the petitioner's only reply (31.5.2007) addressed occupancy, not the theft allegation or quantum, and the assessing officer's own subsequent (albeit procedurally chaotic) self-correction reduced the assessment to the correct 1.5x multiplier (Rs. 21,17,016, down from Rs. 42,78,355), and given the clearly-established theft on the inspection record (a 160 KVA transformer improperly connected via temporary L.T. line to run an ice factory with no sanctioned connection), the Court declined to interfere with the corrected final assessment despite the demonstrated procedural laxity — noting the Court, exercising equity under Article 226, would not assist a demonstrably blameworthy party on technicalities causing loss to public revenue.

UP-2005::8.1(b)(iii).topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-day provisional-bill notice before final assessment

cases.title: Chunni Lal Gupta v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-day provisional-bill notice before final assessment
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires service of a provisional assessment bill with 15 days to reply and a hearing before final assessment. A 'revised bill' issued on the day of the raid, without that procedure, cannot be a final assessment; it is at best provisional, the consumer may file objections to be decided per the Code, and may appeal under Section 127 thereafter.

cases.title: Dr. Munni Lal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-working-day show-cause notice and hearing
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires a show-cause notice giving 15 working days to object and fixing a hearing date before a final assessment; a seven-day notice with no hearing date does not comply. No final order of assessment was passed, so the recovery demand was premature.

UP-2005::8.2.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h)) — effect of a subsequent criminal acquittal on a theft-based civil assessment
UP-2005::8.2.clause: 8.2(X)(g)/(h) (final theft assessment 'subject to adjudication by the court'; mandatory withdrawal of charges/assessment and meter restoration if the court finds theft not established)
UP-2005::8.2.topic: Where a criminal acquittal on the s.135 charge post-dates the appellate order upholding a theft-based assessment, the matter must be remanded to the appellate authority to independently examine Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h) in light of that acquittal

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Where a criminal acquittal on the s.135 charge post-dates the appellate order upholding a theft-based assessment, the matter must be remanded to the appellate authority to independently examine Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h) in light of that acquittal
cases.holding: Since the appellate order (1.4.2010) predated the trial court's acquittal judgment (23.1.2011, disclosed only in the petitioner's rejoinder), the Commissioner had no occasion to consider Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h). The appellate order is modified/partly set aside to the extent that the petitioner's appeal shall be treated as pending before the Commissioner, who must independently and objectively examine the acquittal judgment in light of Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h) and pass a fresh appropriate order, unaffected by the High Court's observations on issues (a)-(c) above (which concerned assessment on the civil/administrative record, not the separate criminal mens rea question).

UP-2005::9.3.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.126(3)) read with U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clauses 8.1(b)(iii), 9.3)
UP-2005::9.3.clause: 9.3 (mode of service of orders/notices) read with 8.1(b)(iii) (right to object to provisional assessment)
UP-2005::9.3.topic: Failure to serve a provisional assessment in the Clause 9.3-prescribed manner deprives the consumer of the s.126(3)/Clause 8.1(b)(iii) right to object; a subsequent demand notice/recovery certificate premised on treating the unserved provisional assessment as final cannot stand without first affording a genuine objection opportunity

cases.title: Shiv Shankar Giri v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
cases.topic: Failure to serve a provisional assessment in the Clause 9.3-prescribed manner deprives the consumer of the s.126(3)/Clause 8.1(b)(iii) right to object; a subsequent demand notice/recovery certificate premised on treating the unserved provisional assessment as final cannot stand without first affording a genuine objection opportunity
cases.holding: No — the licensee's own instructions were silent on whether the provisional assessment was sent by registered or ordinary post, and the consumer denied receiving both the provisional assessment and the subsequent demand notice (sent by ordinary post). This deprived the consumer of the statutory right to object under s.126(3)/Clause 8.1(b)(iii). The Court directed that the petitioner be given six weeks (from receipt of a certified copy of the order and the now-supplied provisional assessment/checking report) to file objections before the Executive Engineer, who must decide them by a reasoned, speaking order after a hearing, preferably within six weeks; recovery proceedings under the impugned citation were stayed until the earlier of a fixed date or disposal of the objections, with recovery to thereafter abide by that decision.

UP-2005::compounding.topic: Theft (s.135) compounded through the Supply Code — theft/UUE-Code linkage

cases.title: Ajmal v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: Theft (s.135) compounded through the Supply Code — theft/UUE-Code linkage
cases.holding: The offence of electricity theft under Section 135 being compoundable, the accused's compounding remedy lies 'as provided under the provisions of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005' — the Code furnishing the machinery through which theft (Section 135) and, cognately, unauthorised use of electricity (Section 126) are assessed and compounded. Pending compounding, as the offence does not entail imprisonment beyond seven years, any arrest must comply with Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A Cr.P.C.; the FIR, disclosing a cognizable offence, was not quashed.
cases.flag: Scope: the case's express Code engagement is the compounding remedy; the operative relief concerned arrest safeguards (s.41(1)(b)/41-A Cr.P.C.). Retained as a node in the theft / unauthorised-use line, which the Supply Code's assessment and compounding machinery governs.

UP-2005::disconnection-notice-requiremen.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (notice requirement for disconnection)
UP-2005::disconnection-notice-requiremen.topic: Permanent disconnection without prior notice, even where premised on alleged unauthorized use at another premises, is arbitrary and unauthorized under the Supply Code; reinstatement is directed, without prejudice to a subsequent show-cause notice

cases.title: Raju v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
cases.topic: Permanent disconnection without prior notice, even where premised on alleged unauthorized use at another premises, is arbitrary and unauthorized under the Supply Code; reinstatement is directed, without prejudice to a subsequent show-cause notice
cases.holding: No — the Supply Code does not permit disconnection of this nature without any notice whatsoever to the consumer. The licensee's own counsel conceded no show-cause notice had been given before the permanent disconnection (carried out 11.6.2024) on the stated ground of unauthorized use at another premises. The Court, without going into the merits of the unauthorized-use allegation, directed reinstallation of the permanently disconnected connection within 7 days, while leaving it open to the licensee to thereafter issue a show-cause notice and proceed in accordance with law, including against the petitioner on the complaint that had been filed.

UP-2005::independent-feeder-definition.code: Tariff Order 2000-01 (issued under s.24, U.P. Electricity Reforms Act, 1999) read with the 'Independent Feeder' definitions in the Electricity Supply Code 2002 and Electricity Supply Code 2005
UP-2005::independent-feeder-definition.clause: 'Independent Feeder' and 'restricted/peak hours' surcharge provisions (HV-2 tariff category, rows 3 and 4 of the Tariff Order 2000-01 table)
UP-2005::independent-feeder-definition.topic: Interpretation of 'independent feeder' (pre-dating its Supply Code definitions) and whether restricted-hours and independent-feeder surcharges under a HV-2 tariff are cumulative

cases.title: Northern Coalfield Ltd. v. Chairman and Managing Director, U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Interpretation of 'independent feeder' (pre-dating its Supply Code definitions) and whether restricted-hours and independent-feeder surcharges under a HV-2 tariff are cumulative
cases.holding: (a) Yes — the restricted-hours surcharge (row 3) and the independent-feeder surcharge (row 4) confer distinct benefits and are cumulative; a consumer availing both must pay a total 30% surcharge, and cannot avoid the restricted-hours surcharge merely by virtue of being on an independent feeder. (b) No — an independent feeder does not cease to be independent because other feeders (serving other consumers) also emanate from the same sub-station; it loses that character only if another consumer is tapped onto the very same feeder. Applying this, the NCL Bina connection (no other consumer on that feeder) was held an independent feeder from a 132 KV sub-station (both surcharges payable, 30% total), while the IWSS Khadia connection (power also tapped to a Kota Basti sub-station on the same feeder, without proven consumer consent) was held not an independent feeder (only the 15% restricted-hours surcharge payable, no independent-feeder surcharge; no penalty for want of prior permission, since the benefit had in fact been extended without objection).

UP-2005::procedure-for-restoration.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.126) read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (restoration-of-connection procedure)
UP-2005::procedure-for-restoration.clause: Restoration procedure following permanent disconnection for non-payment of s.126 dues
UP-2005::procedure-for-restoration.topic: Consent disposal permitting installment payment of s.126 assessment dues, with restoration of a permanently disconnected connection to follow a fresh application under the Supply Code's prescribed procedure

cases.title: Nadeem v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Consent disposal permitting installment payment of s.126 assessment dues, with restoration of a permanently disconnected connection to follow a fresh application under the Supply Code's prescribed procedure
cases.holding: By consent of the parties, the petitioner was permitted to pay the outstanding sum under the recovery certificate in four equal monthly installments (15.8.2024 to 15.11.2024); it was left open to the petitioner to apply for restoration of the electricity connection as per the procedure prescribed under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, with any such application to be considered in accordance with law once the second installment is paid.

UP-2005::tariff-feeder.clause: feeder-based tariff; set-off of repair cost
UP-2005::tariff-feeder.topic: Rural-feeder supply cannot be billed at urban rate; no self-help set-off

cases.title: Harihar Cold Storage v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Rural-feeder supply cannot be billed at urban rate; no self-help set-off
cases.holding: Supply made from a rural feeder cannot be billed at the urban-feeder rate schedule (conceded); the excess is refundable. A consumer who, without authorisation, gets the transformer repaired at his own cost cannot set off that cost against his bills — the remedy is a civil suit.

UPDR1958::3.code: U.P. Government Electrical Undertaking (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958
UPDR1958::3.topic: Recovery demand presupposes a final assessment

cases.title: Dr. Munni Lal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Recovery demand presupposes a final assessment
cases.holding: A demand under Section 3 of the 1958 Dues Recovery Act can be issued only after a final order of assessment is passed; a demand issued before final assessment is without authority and is quashed.

WB-2004::5.2.code: West Bengal Electricity Regulatory Commission (Electricity Supply Code) Regulations, 2004
WB-2004::5.2.topic: Disconnection procedure and the statutory route of objection/appeal under ss.126-127

cases.title: Chairman, West Bengal State Electricity Board & Ors. v. Syed Mukbul Hossain & Ors.
cases.topic: Disconnection procedure and the statutory route of objection/appeal under ss.126-127
cases.holding: Disconnection of supply on a theft allegation must follow the procedure of Regulation 5.2; the consumer's remedies are to object under Section 126(3) before the final assessment and to appeal the final order under Section 127. As the final assessment had already been made, the Court relegated the parties to the statutory appeal, to be decided on merits (including the maintainability/limitation objection), setting aside the costs and interim directions of the High Court and expressing no opinion on merits.
cases.flag: Multi-state: construes the West Bengal Supply Code (2004), not the U.P. 2005 Code. The Supreme Court expressly decided nothing on the merits.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.application: Foundational: Section 126 (civil, no mens rea, wider purposive 'unauthorised use' covering excess load/change of category under Explanation (b)(iv)) and Section 135 (criminal, mens rea) operate in different and distinct fields with no commonality; Sections 126-127 are a complete code, only the final Section 126(3) order is appealable, and Article 226 relief is confined to jurisdictional review.

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.application: Theft (s.135) is a subset of unauthorised use (s.126); a s.126 assessment is available even in theft cases, requiring only civil proof (not proof beyond reasonable doubt/mens rea), and does not merge into or get ousted by the Special Court's s.154(5) civil-liability jurisdiction — both may run in parallel. Applies and extends Seetaram Rice Mill.

lead_authorities.name: Executive Engineer (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill

cases.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Mens rea is irrelevant to a Section 126 civil theft-assessment; it is required only for Section 135 criminal prosecution (agreeing with Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL).

lead_authorities.name: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Anr. v. PVVNL & Ors.

cases.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: Confirms and extends this corpus's tracked doctrine (SCJ-069 Trikoot Iron & Steels) that theft-based assessment proceeds under s.126 (never under s.135 alone), clarifying (contra a misreading of Southco v. Seetaram Rice Mill's 'different fields' language) that s.126 assessment remains mandatory even where a s.135 FIR/Special Court trial is simultaneously pending — the two tracks (assessment for the civil dues, prosecution/civil-liability determination by the Special Court) run in parallel, not in the alternative.

lead_authorities.name: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Company of Orissa Ltd. (Southco) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
M/s Paliwal Alloys (Pvt) Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: Bars the consumer's refund of charges paid without demur and the licensee that only raised bills, never pursuing statutory recovery (s.52 noted).

cases.title: Kapil Gupta v. U.P. Power Corpn. Ltd. & Anr.
cases.application: A writ against a Section 126 assessment is relegated to the Section 127 appeal unless the case falls within the jurisdiction / natural-justice / fundamental-rights exceptions; pure factual disputes go to the appeal.

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar v. State of U.P.
M/s Popcorn Entertainment v. City Industrial Development Corporation

cases.title: M/S Om Ice Factory Thru' Its Partner Satyapal Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr.
cases.application: Confirms and applies the alternative-remedy line (cf. SCJ-040 Kapil Gupta): a writ against a Section 126 assessment is entertained only on a genuine jurisdictional/natural-justice/fundamental-rights challenge; where objections have already been considered by the assessing authority and only the correctness of the assessment on facts/procedure is disputed, the petitioner is relegated to the Section 127 appeal, per Southco v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill (SCJ-041).

lead_authorities.name: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Company of Orissa Ltd. (Southco) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: Palika Towns LLP v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: A party who accepts the beneficial parts of an instrument (here, a Transfer Memorandum/Sale Certificate incorporating lease covenants) cannot simultaneously repudiate its burdens — the doctrine of election/estoppel against approbating and reprobating.

lead_authorities.name: R.N. Gosain v. Yashpal Dhir

cases.title: Anubhav Jaiswal v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: On a legal sub-division of a premises, outstanding electricity dues are divided pro-rata; a purchaser of a portion is liable only for that portion's share.

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: The bar on a new connection for arrears attaches only to the specific premises in default, not to other portions of a building.

cases.title: Amir Ahmad v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: Electricity arrears create a statutory charge on the premises recoverable from a subsequent transferee, including an auction-purchaser on an 'as-is-where-is' basis.

lead_authorities.name: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board

cases.title: Chandra Prakash Gupta v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: The 2005 Code creates the statutory charge that the pre-Code case law lacked: an auction-purchaser cannot escape the previous owner's arrears and must furnish a No-Dues Certificate for a fresh connection.

lead_authorities.name: Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd. v. Gujarat Inns Pvt. Ltd.

cases.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cases.application: Electricity arrears are not a charge on the premises; a transferee/auction-purchaser is liable for the previous owner's dues only where statutory rules or statutory conditions of supply expressly so provide (the refinement underlying the K.C. Ninan line).

lead_authorities.name: Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board
Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Paramount Polymers (P) Ltd.
Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. DVS Steels & Alloys (P) Ltd.

cases.title: Jitendra Kumar Gupta & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.application: 'Outstanding dues' on a premises (including a theft assessment) attach to the premises and are recoverable from a subsequent purchaser, who must obtain a No-Dues Certificate — subject to adjustment against recovery from the original defaulter.

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.application: Apex authority: the Supply Code (under s.50/s.181) can create a statutory charge on the premises for a previous owner's arrears recoverable from a new/subsequent owner; a condition requiring a new owner to clear such arrears is statutory and valid (confirming and extending Haryana SEB v. Hanuman Rice Mills; substantially qualifying Isha Marbles).

lead_authorities.name: Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board

cases.title: M/S Dharti Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. The Managing Director, Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.application: IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION: the K.C. Ninan arrears-run-with-premises doctrine (SCJ-037) is confined to ordinary/non-insolvency transfers; where the premises were acquired through an IBC liquidation auction and the licensee has itself submitted a claim to the Liquidator for the same dues, IBC s.238 overrides the Electricity Act/Supply Code first-charge provisions and the licensee's sole recourse is the IBC waterfall mechanism, not withholding a fresh connection.

lead_authorities.name: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Private Ltd. & Ors.
K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.

cases.title: M/S Rayana Paper Board Industries Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Refines the cluster: absent an express Code provision authorising coercive recovery from a transferee, the licensee's leverage over unpaid dues on a transferred premises is limited to withholding a fresh connection (Clause 4.3), not issuing a land-revenue-style recovery citation against the non-consumer purchaser.

lead_authorities.name: Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. M/s Paramount Polymers Pvt. Ltd.

cases.title: Palika Towns LLP v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: Reinforces, by cross-domain analogy, the arrears-transferee-liability doctrinal cluster already tracked in this corpus (K.C. Ninan/SCJ-037 line): dues (whether electricity or, as here, lease rent) do not automatically constitute a charge on the property, but a specific statutory/regulatory stipulation or an express contractual/auction-notice clause can validly bind a subsequent purchaser to clear the predecessor's arrears as a condition of connection/transfer/recognition.

lead_authorities.name: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. DVS Steels & Alloys Pvt. Ltd.
Haryana State Electricity Board v. Hanuman Rice Mills

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. v. M/s DVS Steels & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: The foundational SC statement of the doctrine underlying this corpus's arrears/transferee-liability cluster (K.C. Ninan/SCJ-037 line, and later applied/qualified in SCJ-054, SCJ-063, SCJ-090, SCJ-098): dues are not a charge on the property in the absence of a stipulation, but a distributor may lawfully condition supply/reconnection on clearance of a predecessor's dues via Clause 4.3(g)/(h)-type provisions, without that being arbitrary or unreasonable.

cases.title: M/S Sartaj Rice Mill Thru' Its Partner Maqsood Ali v. Paschimanchal Vidhyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.application: An assessment finalised by the consumer's own written offer to pay in instalments (accepted by the licensee) cannot later be disputed as never having been finalised; his conduct amounts to acceptance/waiver of a formal final-order requirement.

cases.title: Navi Hasan v. U.P. Power Corporation & Another
cases.application: A demand/assessment order must confront the consumer with adverse material, allow objections, and be a reasoned speaking order after a hearing; a pre-printed proforma order passed in disregard of these requirements (and of prior court directions to that effect) is vitiated for breach of natural justice.

lead_authorities.name: Uma Nath Pandey & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Anr.

cases.title: Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission v. Reliance Energy Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Metered consumption must be billed on actual meter readings; a licensee's supplementary/amended bill raised later on a presumed/average basis (e.g. suspected faulty meter) is not lawful absent due process — resonates with the Clause 5.6/5.9 defective-meter procedure line already established in this corpus (e.g. SCJ-058, SCJ-059, SCJ-071).

cases.title: Islam v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: In a theft/unauthorised-use assessment the burden is on the department to prove commercial or unauthorised use; a farmer need not disprove it where his use is ancillary agricultural use within the sanctioned load.

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.application: CGRF/Ombudsman (creatures of subordinate regulation) have no jurisdiction to review a statutory Assessing Officer's Section 126 assessment or a Section 127 appellate order; the only remedy against such an assessment is under Sections 126/127 themselves. Anchors the later Full Bench holding (SCJ-043 Kisan Cold Storage) that the Ombudsman/CGRF scheme is a distinct consumer-grievance track confined to matters outside Sections 126/127/135 etc.

lead_authorities.name: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Vidyut Lokpal, Lucknow

cases.title: Aruna Bhargava v. PuVVNL & Another
cases.application: A change of forum is not a matter of pure procedure; once proceedings are validly initiated before a forum, that vested right continues despite a later change of jurisdiction, unless the legislature clearly provides otherwise.

lead_authorities.name: CIT v. R. Sharadamma
CIT v. Dhadi Sahu

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.application: Liability for system-upgradation (the system-loading charge) accrues only on actual consumption; a prospective consumer who never draws supply bears no share of it.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.application: A tariff charge conditioned on the consumer opting for a facility (here, protective load) cannot be levied absent that option and the licensee's sanction; it cannot be imposed suo motu on an audit objection.

cases.title: M/S Krown Bakers India Pvt. Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam & Anr.
cases.application: The Clause 5.6 check-meter/testing procedure for a disputed meter is triggered only by the consumer's request; a consumer who has knowledge of a slow-meter finding and does not dispute it or seek testing cannot later invoke Clause 5.6 non-compliance to challenge the consequential bill.

cases.title: Pawan Kumar Agarwal s/o M.P. Agarwal v. State of U.P. thru. Secretary & Ors.
cases.application: Clause 3.4(a)'s enumerated heavy-industry categories requiring mandatory independent-feeder supply are specific and restrictive, not illustrative; other consumers (even at higher loads) have only the Clause 3.4(b) option, not obligation, to seek an independent feeder — directly informs how 'Independent Feeder' provisions are to be read alongside the definitional line traced in SCJ-094 (Northern Coalfield).

cases.title: Mohd. Ashfaq Khan @ Ashfaq Khan v. State of U.P. thru. Addl. Chief Secy., Energy Deptt., Lucknow & 3 Others
cases.application: An occupant/tenant may obtain a fresh electricity connection under Clause 4.4 on furnishing an indemnity bond and proof of possession, even amid a dispute with the property's transferee-owner, subject to licensee verification and without prejudice to civil rights.

cases.title: Seema Mansoor v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & 3 Others
cases.application: A tenant/occupier may obtain a new electricity connection via the Annexure 4.2 indemnity-bond route where the landlord withholds consent; this reinforces and extends the Clause 4.4 occupant-connection principle already tracked in this corpus (SCJ-085, Mohd. Ashfaq Khan) to the new-connection (not just restoration) context, and explicitly holds that landlord-consent refusal cannot be an absolute bar.

cases.title: Priy Shankar Pandey v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: A landowner's Clause 4.5(d) right to object to a supply line over his land is vindicated through the Clause 3, Works of Licensees Rules 2006 resolution mechanism before the District Magistrate/Commissioner of Police, balancing private property rights against public electrification interests.

cases.title: Shivmahraj v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.application: Companion application of the same principle as SCJ-104 (Priy Shankar Pandey v. State of U.P.).

cases.title: Saurabh Agrawal & Another v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: A theft finding premised on a defective/tampered meter requires compliance with Clause 5.6(d)'s testing procedure (notice, opportunity to be present, consumer's right to dispute per 5.6(c)); non-compliance (no MRI, no proper laboratory testing) undermines the evidentiary basis for both the assessment and any criminal prosecution.

lead_authorities.name: M/s Modern Rice Mill v. Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
Smt. Amrawati Devi v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.

cases.title: Satya Narayan v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. thru. its Managing Director & Others
cases.application: The Clause 6.15/s.56(2) two-year recovery bar is not passive — it obliges the licensee to actively pursue notice-and-disconnection under Clause 4.36 within that window; prolonged inaction (here, ~12 years) forfeits recoverability, and Clause 4.38(c)'s permanent-disconnection-affidavit requirement cannot be read in isolation to override this.

cases.title: Madarsa Dargah Aaliya Islamiya Shareef Nagar & Anr. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: A dispute solely over quantification of a demand is relegated to the Clause 6.5B authority for a reasoned determination, rather than being adjudicated in writ jurisdiction.

cases.title: Sanjay Rizvi v. M.D. Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. & Others
cases.application: Before an assessing officer concludes that unauthorised use of electricity has occurred, Clause 6.8's inspection-report/show-cause/hearing/speaking-order procedure must be substantially followed, given the seriousness of the allegation; a provisional assessment lacking authentic verification data (e.g. unperformed MRI testing that the licensee's own procedure contemplates) is impugnable.

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: Om Prakash v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: Billing grievances against a licensee are to be routed through the Clause 7.10 Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (and Ombudsman on appeal), a specific licensee-grievance mechanism distinct from and preferred over the general District Consumer Forum route — reinforcing the s.42(5)/(6)-equivalent individual-grievance routing principle already tracked in this corpus (SCJ-076, MERC v. Reliance Energy).

cases.title: Priya Prem v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. & 4 Others
cases.application: Companion application of the CGRF-routing principle already tracked in this corpus (SCJ-076, SCJ-096) — new-connection and delay-penalty grievances under s.43/Clause 4.4/7.7.2 are likewise routed through the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum rather than decided directly by the writ court.

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Confirms and applies the specific-over-general canon (from Mohit Paper Mills) that Clauses 8.1/8.2, not Clause 6.8, govern theft-based (s.135) assessment, including the mandatory 15-working-day notice and 1.5x (not 3x) tariff multiplier.

lead_authorities.name: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Another v. PVVNL & Others

cases.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
cases.application: After a consumer files objections to a theft-related provisional assessment, Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires an actual personal hearing before any final assessment can be made; a bare 'final notice' reiterating the provisional figure, without a hearing or reasoned order, is unenforceable — reinforcing the corpus's cluster of s.126/Clause 8.1 procedural-strictness rulings (SCJ-069, SCJ-087, SCJ-092, SCJ-111).

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others
Kamil v. State of U.P. & Others
Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.

cases.title: Latif v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.application: The Clause 6.8 inspection-notice-hearing-final-order sequence is mandatory before any unauthorised-use assessment; a demand raised by bypassing this procedure (e.g. directly under the 1958 Recovery of Dues Act) is illegal, following and applying Ashok Kumar v. State of U.P.

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: M/S Kissan Chilling Udyog & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.application: Extends the Ashok Kumar/Clause 6.8 line: a theft assessment fails not only for skipping the prescribed procedure but also where the notice/final order misreads or mischaracterises the checking report itself (e.g. conflating a test/double meter's findings with the main meter's), since the consumer is thereby condemned on a factual basis the evidence does not support.

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: A subsequent criminal acquittal on the s.135 charge, per Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h), mandatorily requires withdrawal of the theft-based civil assessment and meter restoration — where such acquittal post-dates an appellate order, remand is required for the appellate authority to apply this clause.

cases.title: Shiv Shankar Giri v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
cases.application: A provisional assessment cannot be treated as final for want of objections unless the licensee can establish it was served in the manner Clause 9.3 prescribes; failure to do so, especially where the consumer denies receipt, deprives the consumer of the s.126(3)/Clause 8.1(b)(iii) objection right and vitiates a subsequent recovery based on that unserved assessment.

cases.title: Mohamdabad Cold Storage Private Ltd. (& Anr.) v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Clause 6.5(b)'s heading ('Disputed Bills and Arrears') does not confine its scope; a supplementary bill grounded in a disputed meter reading is a disputed bill within the clause — resonates with the marginal-heading-not-an-aid-to-construction principle already tracked in this corpus (SCJ-059/060, Chandler v. DPP line).

cases.title: Mother India Refrigeration Industries (& Anr.) v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Companion application of the same principle as SCJ-083.

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.application: The Code's grievance forum (CGRF/Ombudsman) and the Act's overriding clause do not cover a claim of tortious damages for wrongful disconnection; such claims lie before the Lok Adalat / consumer fora.

cases.title: Divisional Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-I v. Raman Singh & Another
cases.application: The Supply Code and its CGRF/Ombudsman forum cover consumer grievances, not a non-consumer's tort-damages claim against the licensee; such claims lie before the Permanent Lok Adalat as a public-utility-service dispute.

lead_authorities.name: Bar Council of India v. Union of India
S.N. Pandey v. Union of India

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: The Supply Code/EA scheme (and the s.145 civil-court bar) govern consumer disputes; a non-consumer's tort-damages claim for electrocution is a public-utility-service dispute the Permanent Lok Adalat may decide.

lead_authorities.name: Bar Council of India v. Union of India
United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Ajay Sinha

cases.title: Jharkhand State Electricity Board & Others v. M/s Ramkrishna Forging Limited
cases.application: Supply Code regulations, being terms dictated by a monopoly supplier, are to be liberally interpreted in favour of the consumer; load-enhancement agreements are treated as continuations of the initial agreement.

cases.title: Om Prakash s/o Gauri Shankar v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Payment of a s.152(3) compounding fee for theft is distinct from, and does not extinguish, the consumer's separate civil liability for electricity actually consumed; recovery notices for consumption dues survive compounding — a companion principle to this corpus's theft/126 procedural-strictness line, clarifying that compounding addresses only the criminal offence.

cases.title: M/S Three Star Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 5 Ors.
cases.application: Delay/laches of decades bars a consumer from claiming the benefit of a favourable judgment obtained by other, timely litigants on the same point.

lead_authorities.name: New Delhi Municipal Council v. Pan Singh & Others
Yunus v. State of Maharashtra & Others

cases.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Rahamatullah Khan alias Rahamjulla
cases.application: The two-year bar in s.56(2) restricts only the coercive remedy of disconnection; the licensee may still raise a supplementary demand and pursue other modes of recovery (including within limitation from discovery of a mistake).

cases.title: Devendra Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: A landlord-tenant or ownership dispute is not a ground to disconnect a validly sanctioned electricity connection; the Code's new-connection procedure cannot be turned to that use.

cases.title: Dipali Dey (Baxi) v. Mira Das
cases.application: A tenant in possession is not to be deprived of electric supply on account of a landlord-tenant dispute; supply is restored (here by civil injunction pending the suit).

cases.title: Divya Sahani v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.application: A pending ownership/property dispute is not a ground to refuse or disconnect a connection; a connection confers no title, so the supply question is independent of the title dispute.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Private Limited & Ors.
cases.application: Electricity dues are not automatically a 'secured interest'/first charge under the IBC merely by virtue of a Supply Code recovery-as-arrears-of-land-revenue mechanism; secured-creditor status depends on whether a security interest was actually created (by contract clause or operation of law) and, if so, the claim is processed within the s.53 waterfall, not outside/above the IBC.

lead_authorities.name: State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Ltd.

cases.title: Mohd Usman Ansari v. Chairman, Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. & 4 Others
cases.application: A recovery certificate founded on an ex-parte provisional s.126 assessment, made without following the Supply Code's assessment/hearing procedure, cannot be coercively enforced until the consumer is given a hearing and a reasoned final assessment is passed.

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.application: Excess load or appliance installation within/around the contracted load is not 'unauthorised use' under Section 126 (para 6.9 of the Code); the remedy is the tariff's additional Fixed Charge, not a theft/UUE assessment.

cases.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Rahamatullah Khan alias Rahamjulla
cases.application: Electricity charges become 'first due' when the bill is issued quantifying them, though liability to pay arises on consumption; the limitation clock under s.56(2) starts from billing.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Private Limited & Ors.
cases.application: A distribution licensee's dues do not automatically rank as 'government dues' under s.53(1)(e)/(f) IBC merely because of state shareholding in the licensee; the licensee remains a distinct juristic entity in a liberalised, privately-contestable sector.

lead_authorities.name: Municipal Commissioner of Dum Dum Municipality v. Indian Tourism Development Corporation

cases.title: Divisional Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-I v. Raman Singh & Another
cases.application: Electricity distribution is a hazardous activity; the licensee is under a statutory duty to maintain its installations and lines so that passers-by (human or animal) are not harmed.

lead_authorities.name: Shakuntala Devi v. Delhi Electric Supply Undertaking

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: A distribution company has an onerous duty to maintain its devices and to disconnect current from the sub-station in a storm; failure to do so is negligence founding a damages claim.

cases.title: Narendra Singh Panwar v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.application: The s.14 IBC moratorium and a resolution plan's discharge of the Corporate Debtor do not extinguish a Director's independent personal-guarantor liability for the company's electricity dues under Clause 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 of the Supply Code — a distinct sub-doctrine within this corpus's IBC/electricity-arrears cluster (cf. SCJ-054 Dharti Agro Industries, where IBC s.238 barred recovery from the licensee itself post-liquidation; SCJ-063's PVVNL v. Raman Ispat line on arrears running with premises/against the Corporate Debtor). Here the qualification cuts the other way: IBC discharge of the Corporate Debtor does not reach a Director's separate, co-extensive personal guarantee.

lead_authorities.name: State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan
Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India
Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union of India

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Private Limited & Ors.
cases.application: Once liquidation commences, IBC s.238 overrides the Electricity Act's ss.173/174 non-obstante recovery provisions and the Supply Code's Clause 4.3/6.15 mechanism; a licensee cannot independently attach/auction a corporate debtor's assets for electricity dues outside the IBC's collective process — directly confirms and elevates to Supreme Court authority the qualification to the arrears-run-with-the-premises doctrine already tracked via SCJ-054 (Dharti Agro Industries) and the NCLT/NCLAT ruling cited in SCJ-090 (Narendra Singh Panwar).

lead_authorities.name: Sundaresh Bhatt, Liquidator of ABG Shipyard v. Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs
Duncans Industries Ltd. v. AJ Agrochem

cases.title: M/S Dharti Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. The Managing Director, Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.application: Section 238 of the IBC, being a later special enactment with a non-obstante clause, overrides sectoral statutes with their own non-obstante/first-charge provisions (Electricity Act ss.173-174; also applied to the Customs Act and the Tea Act in other SC rulings) once liquidation/moratorium proceedings are triggered and the sectoral authority has participated in them.

lead_authorities.name: Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank & Anr.

cases.title: M/S Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Anr. v. PVVNL & Ors.
cases.application: Where the consumer's own meter cannot yield a reading due to physical impossibility (fire, theft), a reliably maintained outside/check meter may exceptionally found billing, applying the impossibility maxims.

lead_authorities.name: Inter College Kusmaul, Gorakhpur & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.

cases.title: M/S Shri Parasnath Alloys (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Clause 3.4(d)(ii)'s consent requirement for tapping an independent feeder runs to the consumer who funded the feeder's construction (the 'original consumer'), not to every downstream tapping consumer who paid only its own connecting-line cost; a downstream consumer can acquire a consent right only by itself having obtained the true original consumer's consent and shared the feeder's cost (Kesarwani Sheetalaya).

lead_authorities.name: M/s Kesarwani Sheetalaya & Others v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
M/s Shiv Flour and Rice Mills v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: Northern Coalfield Ltd. v. Chairman and Managing Director, U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: A feeder remains 'independent' notwithstanding other consumers being fed from other feeders off the same sub-station; it loses independence only if another consumer is tapped onto the very same feeder — the operative test for 'Independent Feeder' both under this pre-Code tariff interpretation and, by extension, informing how the term is later defined in the Electricity Supply Code 2002/2005.

cases.title: M/S Santosh Preservation Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr.
cases.application: Clause 5.6(c)(iii)'s independent-laboratory option is triggered only when the tampering/defect finding is derived from a test report; it has no application where tampering is visibly patent at inspection, distinguishing Mohd. Sagir and Amrawati Devi (ambiguous, test-report-dependent tampering).

lead_authorities.name: Mohd. Sagir v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.

cases.title: Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission v. Reliance Energy Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: A State Electricity Regulatory Commission cannot adjudicate individual consumers' billing grievances or issue a blanket refund direction without a proper s.128 investigation; individual grievances go through the s.42(5) Forum and s.42(6) Ombudsman.

cases.title: Kripa Shanker v. State of U.P. Thru. Distt. Collector, Unnao & Ors.
cases.application: A consumer unable to pay an outstanding bill in one go may apply under Clause 6.14 of the Supply Code for installment payment; the Executive Engineer must consider and decide such an application expeditiously.

cases.title: M/S Hind Industries Limited v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.application: Interest on a sum wrongfully retained/evaded (e.g. under Clause 8.1 of the Supply Code) is compensatory, not penal or confiscatory.

lead_authorities.name: Wig Brothers (Builders & Engineers) (P) Ltd. & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.

cases.title: M/S Hind Industries Limited v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.application: A time-bound interim protection order automatically lapses on expiry of its term; a consumer cannot rely on its continued existence, or on an unrelated pending application, to justify years of non-payment of an assessed sum.

cases.title: Mrs Rajendra Kumar Sharma v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: Where a defective assessment is set aside for procedural non-compliance, the Court may order interim restoration of supply on the consumer furnishing security, subject to the outcome of a properly conducted fresh assessment.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.application: For determining which version of Section 126 (deposit condition, assessment rate) applies, the operative date is the date of the FINAL assessment, not the provisional assessment or the date the cause of action arose.

lead_authorities.name: Sri Bhagwan Gupta v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company Ltd.

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.application: When the Supply Code / Section 126 deems assessed energy to be consumed, the fiction must be given full effect and the assessed units treated as sales.

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.application: Deposits taken as part of the estimate are refundable unless the licensee proves the actual expenditure reasonably incurred; unproved heads must be refunded.

cases.title: Northern Coalfield Ltd. v. Chairman and Managing Director, U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: A licensee's own circular/notification cannot alter or vary a tariff duly approved by the Regulatory Commission; in case of inconsistency, the Commission-approved tariff order prevails.

lead_authorities.name: LML Ltd., Kanpur v. State of U.P.

cases.title: M/S Venus Stone Crushing Co. & Anr. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: The mandatory seven-day pre-testing notice requirement (Amrawati Devi) is now final law, the Supreme Court having dismissed the SLP against it; non-compliance renders the test report unusable.

lead_authorities.name: Smt. Amrawati Devi v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr.

cases.title: M/S Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
cases.application: A clause's marginal heading (e.g. 'Defective Meters' for Clause 5.6) does not restrict its substantive scope; general principle of statutory construction applied to a Supply Code clause.

lead_authorities.name: Chandroji Rao v. CIT
Padmaraje R. Kadambande v. CIT
Guntaiah & Others v. Hambamma & Others

cases.title: Mohamdabad Cold Storage Private Ltd. (& Anr.) v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Where a billing dispute turns on the accuracy of a meter/transformer reading, the consumer must first invoke the Clause 5.6 testing procedure (and thereafter the Electrical Inspector) rather than approach the writ court directly; the writ challenge is premature until that statutory route is exhausted.

lead_authorities.name: Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Undertaking v. Laffans (India) Pvt. Ltd.

cases.title: Mother India Refrigeration Industries (& Anr.) v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Companion application of the same principle as SCJ-083.

lead_authorities.name: Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Undertaking v. Laffans (India) Pvt. Ltd.

cases.title: M/S Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
cases.application: Testing of a disputed meter by its own manufacturer (e.g. Secure Meters Ltd.) does not satisfy the Code's requirement of testing at an 'independent laboratory'; such testing is inherently biased and cannot be relied upon to sustain an unauthorised-use assessment. Followed by later cases (see also SCJ-051 line applying the same technical background).

lead_authorities.name: M/s JMD Alloys Limited v. Bihar State Electricity Board

cases.title: M/S Venus Stone Crushing Co. & Anr. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Reaffirms (following Modern Rice Mill, SCJ-059, and JMD Alloys) that a meter manufacturer's own lab is not an 'independent laboratory'; extends the point with a burden-of-proof holding that the licensee must affirmatively prove the consumer (not an intervening cause after the meter left his custody) caused any tampering found.

lead_authorities.name: M/s Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
M/s JMD Alloys Limited v. Bihar State Electricity Board

cases.title: Lala Ram Batham v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam & Ors.
cases.application: A disputed/implausible meter reading is to be resolved by a Clause 6.5 representation before the licensee, decided by a speaking order after inspection of the meter, rather than by the writ court on merits.

cases.title: M/S Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
cases.application: Minimum consumption/guarantee charges for a disconnection period are chargeable only if the disconnection is attributable to the consumer's own fault; a licensee-caused or unresolved-fault disconnection cannot ground such a demand.

cases.title: Dhirendra Kumar Chaudhary v. State of U.P. & 5 Others
cases.application: The Establishment must prove disciplinary charges by evidence led through a Presenting Officer; charges are not proof of themselves, and material used behind the delinquent's back vitiates the inquiry.

lead_authorities.name: State of U.P. v. Saroj Kumar Sinha
Roop Singh Negi v. Punjab National Bank
State of Uttaranchal v. Kharak Singh

cases.title: Harihar Cold Storage v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.application: Minimum-guarantee (and like) charges cannot be levied for a period in which supply failed for a reason attributable to the licensee; the obligation to pay is tied to the licensee's maintaining the minimum standard of supply.

lead_authorities.name: Raymond Ltd. v. M.P. Electricity Board

cases.title: Raju v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
cases.application: Permanent disconnection of electricity supply — even where grounded in an allegation of unauthorized use — requires prior notice/show-cause opportunity under the Supply Code; disconnection without notice is arbitrary and unauthorized, warranting reinstatement without prejudice to a subsequent lawful show-cause process.

cases.title: Gaurav Sharma v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: A genuine occupier (including a family member in separate possession) has a statutory right under s.43(1) to a connection and may furnish an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2) where the owner's NOC is unavailable; the bond only excludes trespassers/house-grabbers.

lead_authorities.name: Seema Mansoor v. U.P. Power Corporation
Chandu Khamaru v. Nayan Malik

cases.title: Husna Bano v. State of U.P. & 9 Others
cases.application: A tenant/occupier unable to obtain the owner's NOC may obtain a connection on an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2); the bond is not a title document, and a landlord-tenant/succession dispute is no ground to deny the basic necessity of electricity.

lead_authorities.name: Gaurav Sharma v. State of U.P.
Chandu Khamaru v. Nayan Malik

cases.title: Dr. Ashok Kumar Sharma & Another v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: The right of a tenant/occupier to a connection under the Code presupposes authorised occupation; it does not extend to a person against whom an unstayed eviction decree operates. (Qualifies the tenant-occupier entitlement recognised in Anand Kumar / SCJ-006.)

lead_authorities.name: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P.

cases.title: Kisan Cold Storage & Ice Factory v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. (Full Bench reference)
cases.application: Foundational Full Bench ruling: the Section 42(5)-(7) Forum/Ombudsman grievance scheme is for the consumer alone; a Regulation cannot extend the Ombudsman remedy to the Distribution Licensee, as that would make the subordinate regulation inconsistent with the parent Act.

lead_authorities.name: Jindal Poly Films Limited v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission

cases.title: M.K. Pathak, Executive Engineer v. The Electricity Ombudsman & Ors.
cases.application: Confirms, on Clause 7.10 of the Supply Code and Section 42(5)-(7), that only the consumer (not the licensee) may approach the CGRF/Ombudsman — an independent DB ruling reaching the same conclusion later confirmed by the Full Bench in Kisan Cold Storage (SCJ-043) construing the parallel UPERC Regulations, 2007 provision.

cases.title: M/S Three Star Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 5 Ors.
cases.application: Acceptance of a licensee's One Time Settlement covering all pending disputes estops the consumer from later reviving any one of those disputes.

cases.title: Chunni Lal Gupta v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: A final theft/assessment bill cannot be raised without the Code's mandatory provisional-bill notice, 15-day reply window and hearing; a same-day 'revised bill' is only provisional.

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.application: The Code's billing/disconnection timeline (15-day bill dispatch plus notice) is mandatory; a truncated bill and premature disconnection are illegal.

cases.title: Dr. Munni Lal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: A final theft assessment requires the Code's mandatory 15-working-day show-cause notice and a hearing; recovery cannot precede a final assessment.

cases.title: Gauri Shankar Gupta v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: A proper Section 126 / Clause 8.1 assessment made after notice and hearing is a precondition to any recovery of theft dues; recovery under the 1958 Act cannot precede a valid final assessment.

cases.title: Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.application: In the consumer/electricity-theft context, the statutory 'reasonable opportunity of hearing' (s.126(3)) includes a personal hearing before a final assessment; taking note of written objections alone is insufficient.

lead_authorities.name: Transmission Corpn. of A.P. Ltd. v. Sri Rama Krishna Rice Mill
Khem Chand v. Union of India

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: Applied against a distribution licensee: the procedural prerequisite (amending the agreement) is deemed waived within a reasonable time of the consumer's request.

lead_authorities.name: M.K. Shah Engineers & Contractors v. State of M.P.
Kusheshwar Prasad Singh v. State of Bihar
Mrutunjay Pani v. Narmada Bala Sasmal
Chairman, SBI v. M.J. James
Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (Pvt.) Ltd.

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: The s.2(15) 'consumer' definition's broad second limb (premises connected for receiving electricity) extends civil assessment liability for theft to a property owner even where an unsubstantiated tenancy is claimed, though criminal mens rea remains a separate question — an important gloss on who bears assessment liability, complementing this corpus's transferee/occupant-liability cluster (SCJ-090, SCJ-098).

cases.title: M/S Birla Aircon v. District Magistrate, Meerut & Ors.
cases.application: The Supply Code's 'premises' definition (area/portion sanctioned to a single consumer) bounds the scope of recovery/sealing against a defaulting consumer; disputes about whether a third party's distinct premises were wrongly included are fact-specific and go to the recovery authority (Collector), not the writ court.

cases.title: M/S Dev Prayag Paper Mill (Pvt.) & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors. (batch of ~90 connected writ petitions)
cases.application: The s.47(5)/Clause 4.20(l) security exemption for consumers willing to take supply through a prepayment meter operates only once such meters are actually available for that consumer category; unavailability (as for HT consumers) leaves the licensee's ordinary power to demand security under s.47(1)-(4) intact. Followed and agreed with the Telangana/AP High Court's parallel ruling in Sarwottam Ispat.

lead_authorities.name: Sarwottam Ispat Ltd. v. Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Ltd. & Ors.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.application: Reasonable opportunity of hearing before a theft-based Section 126 assessment is governed by Clauses 6.8(b)(i)/6.8(c)(iii)/8.1(b) of the Supply Code; substantial compliance (even via a court-directed representation) condones a procedural defect at the provisional stage.

lead_authorities.name: Khem Chand v. Union of India
Transmission Corporation of A.P. Ltd. v. Sri Rama Krishna Rice Mill

cases.title: Navi Hasan v. U.P. Power Corporation & Another
cases.application: An assessing officer who withdraws/recalls a demand order during pending litigation must disclose the statutory power (under the Electricity Act or Supply Code, 2005) exercised to do so; failure to do so is prima facie misconduct.

cases.title: Shyam Ferrous Ltd. Gopal Nagar v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.application: Service of a demand notice by registered post to the address on the licensee's records is deemed sufficient under Explanation 1 to s.3 of the 1958 Dues Recovery Act, regardless of a bare denial of receipt.

lead_authorities.name: Vishanji Tokarsi v. Collector, Kanpur Nagar

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.application: A Regulator cannot, at the truing-up stage, change the methodology or principles of the initial tariff determination; doing so is an impermissible retrospective revision of a quasi-judicial tariff order.

lead_authorities.name: PTC India Ltd. v. CERC

cases.title: Chairman, West Bengal State Electricity Board & Ors. v. Syed Mukbul Hossain & Ors.
cases.application: Where the statutory appeal under Section 127 against a final assessment is available and has been invoked, the parties are relegated to it (with maintainability/limitation left to the appellate authority) rather than to writ/appellate interference on merits.

cases.title: Chandrika v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: A billing-correctness dispute is to be pursued through the Code's grievance channel (Clause 6.5) before the Competent Authority, not by writ, the writ court granting only interim protection on part-deposit.

cases.title: Dr. Santosh Kumar Awasthi v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: Against a final theft-assessment order, the consumer is relegated to the s.127 / Clause 6.8(d) appeal (with the half-deposit), the writ court giving only limitation protection and a short recovery stay.

cases.title: Devendra Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: Supply of electricity is necessary for a life with dignity; disconnection for reasons not authorised by the Act/Code, for malafide purposes, violates Article 21.

cases.title: Divya Sahani v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.application: Supply of electricity to an occupant is fundamental to living with dignity under Article 21; refusal/disconnection on extraneous grounds offends it.

cases.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: An inordinate gap between provisional and final assessment (here, over two years) requires a fresh notice/hearing before the final assessment is passed; failure to do so violates natural justice regardless of the consumer's earlier default in objecting.

cases.title: Mrs Rajendra Kumar Sharma v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: A final assessment under s.126 must engage with the consumer's objections and record findings after a fixed hearing date, per Clauses 6.8/8.1; failure to do so vitiates the assessment and any recovery founded on it — reinforcing the procedural-strictness line already tracked in this corpus for theft/final-assessment orders (e.g. SCJ-069, SCJ-071).

cases.title: Pawan Kumar Laur v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: An officer of a distribution licensee authorised under s.135(2) is competent to lodge an FIR for theft of electricity under s.135(1); this authority is not displaced by unproven allegations of malafide timing.

lead_authorities.name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal

cases.title: Mobin Ahamad v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.application: A cognizable s.135 FIR will not be quashed, but arrest must comply with Cr.P.C. s.41(1)(b)/41-A safeguards where the offence carries under 7 years, and a compoundable s.135 offence's remedy lies via the Supply Code/s.152 route rather than quashing.

cases.title: Mohamad Aslam v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.application: Companion application of the same principle as SCJ-081.

cases.title: Shyam Ferrous Ltd. Gopal Nagar v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.application: The s.56(2)/Clause 6.15 two-year recovery-limitation bar applies only prospectively to post-2003-Act liabilities; pre-2003-Act liabilities remain governed by s.24 of the 1910 Act (no limitation on demand/recovery power) via s.6 of the General Clauses Act — an important temporal-scope qualification on the recovery-limitation doctrine tracked elsewhere in this corpus (SCJ-111, SCJ-113, SCJ-119), distinguishing and narrowing the Paliwal Alloys/Satya Narain line where the underlying liability predates the 2003 Act.

lead_authorities.name: Kusumam Hotels (P) Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board
M/s Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board

cases.title: M/S. Kamla Cold Storage And Ice Factory v. M.V.V.N.L. & Anr.
cases.application: Section 62(6) interest is confined to genuine overcharging above the determined tariff; a rebate under the tariff order is a bill-level concession, and its delayed crediting does not attract s.62(6) interest.

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. M/s L.M.L. Limited & Ors.
cases.application: A licensee must give protective, fair treatment to a Relief Undertaking / Sick Industrial Company (current dues only, arrears in instalments, no coercive disconnection) and cannot defeat an agreed load reduction by legalese; the Supply Code is applied to aid revival.

lead_authorities.name: Modern Syntax (I) Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Tribunal, Jaipur

cases.title: Saurabh Agrawal & Another v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: Where a licensee itself assesses and fully recovers disputed consumption as slow-metering charges under Clause 5.6(c)(ii) (a civil, non-theft remedy), and a s.127 appellate authority conclusively finds s.135 inapplicable on the same facts, a parallel/continuing s.135 theft prosecution on the identical inspection report is an abuse of process.

cases.title: M/S Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
cases.application: Where the Supply Code's assessment-rate provision is discrepant with the governing statute (Section 126(6)), the statute prevails.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.application: A statutory consumer grievance forum (CGRF/Ombudsman) must decide the consumer's dispute on merits and cannot abdicate by relegating the parties to an arbitration clause; the statutory remedy is additional, by right of election, not ousted by the agreement.

lead_authorities.name: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Essar Power Ltd.

cases.title: Shyam Ferrous Ltd. Gopal Nagar v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.application: For limitation purposes, an electricity charge/penalty 'first becomes due' only when a bill/demand is actually raised (and unpaid), not from the date of the underlying default/violation — a licensee's delayed billing (for legitimate reasons, e.g. awaiting correction of an earlier erroneous waiver) does not by itself extinguish recovery rights.

lead_authorities.name: MCD v. H.D. Shourie
NDMC v. Karam Chandra Thapar & Brothers Pvt. Ltd.

cases.title: Satya Narayan v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. thru. its Managing Director & Others
cases.application: Provisions of the Supply Code must be construed together, in context, not in isolation — a specific clause (Clause 4.38(c)) cannot be relied upon divorced from the licensee's parallel obligations (Clause 4.36/6.15).

lead_authorities.name: Grasim Industries Ltd. v. Collector of Customs
Zameer Ahmed Latifur Rehman Sheikh v. State of Maharashtra

cases.title: Northern Coalfield Ltd. v. Chairman and Managing Director, U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Where power is taken during restricted hours with (implicit or express) permission/acquiescence of the licensee, only the tariff surcharge applies; taking power surreptitiously/by theft during restricted hours instead attracts penalty under the theft provisions, not merely a surcharge.

lead_authorities.name: Prachi Leathers v. UPPCL

cases.title: M/S Shokumbhari Pulp & Paper Mills Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & 3 Others (with connected petitions)
cases.application: A revised tariff takes effect only from seven days after its publication (Clause 3.8 of the Supply Code / s.24(7) Reforms Act / Regulation 139); it cannot be applied retrospectively to an earlier date, following Binani Zinc's presumption against retrospective statutory/regulatory effect.

lead_authorities.name: Binani Zinc Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.

cases.title: M/S Trikoot Iron & Steels Castings Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.application: Foundational clarification for the corpus: a theft-based assessment (Clause 8.1-8.3 of the Code) remains a Section 126 assessment appealable under Section 127; it is never treated as a non-appealable Section 135 order. Confirms and extends SCJ-011 (Chairman, WBSEB v. Syed Mukbul Hossain) and the Clause 6.8/8.1 line (Ashok Kumar, Mohit Paper Mills).

lead_authorities.name: Chairman, West Bengal State Electricity Board & Ors. v. Syed Mukbul Hossain & Ors.
Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: M/S Urmila Oil Industries v. U.P. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam & Ors.
cases.application: An assessment cannot be grounded merely on the 'possibility' of theft inferred from a load pattern (e.g. MRI-recorded nil night load); the assessing authority must give specific, disclosed reasons and follow the Clause 6.8 procedure, engaging with the consumer's explanation on its merits (cf. SCJ-060 Mohit Paper Mills: theft must be established, not presumed).

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: M/S Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Anr. v. PVVNL & Ors.
cases.application: A theft assessment under para 8.1(b)(iv) of the Code requires cogent, disclosed evidence of unauthorised use; an unexplained late-period divergence between the billing meter and untested outside check-meters (which otherwise tracked the billing meter closely) does not suffice, and an unsupported technical suggestion at hearing cannot cure the evidentiary gap.

cases.title: Ajmal v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.application: A compoundable Section 135 theft offence is to be compounded under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 procedure; the Code supplies the enforcement / compounding machinery for theft (and, cognately, unauthorised use under Section 126).

cases.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: Where full arguments on the underlying theft assessment have already been made and the 'without jurisdiction' exception is invoked, the Court may examine the record on merits (checking report, MRI report) to see if the assessment is patently illegal, rather than mechanically relegating to the s.127 appeal; physical/MRI indicators of direct extraction, even without a red-handed catch, satisfy Ashok Kumar's notice-of-manner requirement.

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: Aruna Bhargava v. PuVVNL & Another
cases.application: The right of appeal is a substantive right that vests when the original (here, assessment) proceedings are initiated, governed by the law then in force, and is not taken away by a later statute unless expressly or by necessary intendment; a new pre-deposit condition cannot be imposed on such a vested appeal.

lead_authorities.name: Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry
Ramesh Singh v. Cinta Devi
Shiv Shakti Coop. Housing Society v. Swaraj Developers

cases.title: Narendra Singh Panwar v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.application: A challenge to the vires of a Supply Code clause (here Clause 4.3(f)(v), on the ground Directors fall outside the s.2(15) 'consumer' definition) cannot be entertained where raised only in oral rejoinder submissions without any foundation laid in the writ petition itself.

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: A compounding/assessment amount paid without protest or contemporaneous objection cannot later be assailed as realised under coercion.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. v. M/s DVS Steels & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: A consumer who voluntarily pays disputed dues as a condition for obtaining a benefit (here, a fresh connection), pursuant to its own undertaking, cannot later claim a refund based on a subsequent regulatory order that merely restrains future demands, absent an express refund direction — the payment remains refundable only per the terms of the original undertaking.

cases.title: Sanjay Rizvi v. M.D. Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. & Others
